summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the money lending investment could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal held favour with the Appellate Tribunal. In doing so, the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth tax Officer appealed to this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of s.2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee, on the valuation date". [310C] 2.1 In the instant case, the assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of section 7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Income Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valu date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset.

The appellants are the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmarmar Oiteral do Predio ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and therefore a suit filed for a mere declaration simpliciter could not lie. On appeal by the defendants, the Appellate Court concurred with the findings recorded by the two courts below and dismissed the appeal on March 25, 1986. The High Court allowed the appeals and reversed the decree of the Trial Court with no order as to costs. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the suit was barred by res judicata in view of the dismissal of the former suit No. 157/68. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Civil Court undoubtedly had jurisdiction under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure to try and grant eviction till the Fifth Amendment became effective. After that amendment came into force, the provisions of the Act became applicable to the lands in question which were primarily used for growing coconut trees and receiving produce therefrom. By virtue of Section 7 any question whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court stood ousted by section 58(2) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. [1024G 1025A] 2.1 The suit in question was instituted on May 6, 1974 i.e. before the Fifth amendment was brought into force. Thus the amendment came to force during the pendency of the litigation. No provision is made in the Act in that behalf. The jurisdiction of Civil Court is specifically barred by sub section (2)of Section 58 from settling, deciding or dealing with any question which is required to he settled, decided or dealt with by the Tahsildar. [ 1026C] 2:2 In the instant case, the plaintiff came to court contending that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by Section 9 of Act, defendant No 1 had dispossessed him by an act of trespass. He, therefore, sought the Court 's assistance to protect his possession by a prohibitory injunction.

The petitioners are working as carpenters. They are termed as daily rated employees. In the petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have equal pay for equal work. The Corporation resisted the claim on the ground that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act and that the petitioners are given all benefits due to them under various labour legislations. It was also stated that the peti tioners are supplied with the necessary tools for carrying out their work and also working uniforms like aprons and overalls. The financial aspect of the Corporation is stated to be not encouraging, and indeed it is disappointing. It has suffered huge loss and the total losses accumulated hitherto is Rs.69 lakhs. However, for the purpose of preserv ing and promoting traditional arts and crafts, the Corpora tion has been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that in service merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration and she or she learns also by experience as much as by other means. Apart from that, the Court has expressly observed that the higher pay scale to avoid stagnation or resultant frustration for lack of promotional avenues may also be allowed. The petitioners are employed by a company incorporated under the . They cannot claim wages payable to their counterparts in government service. Secondly, it may be noted that the Petitioners are carpenterers; better called as craftsmen. By the general description of their job, one cannot come to the conclusion that every carpenter or craftsman is equal to the other in the performance of his work. In view of the aforesaid principles, the petitioners ' case is rested. The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. The princi ple was incorporated only under Article 39(d) of the Consti tution as a Directive Principle of State Policy. It follows naturally that equal pay must depend upon the nature of the work done, it cannot be judged by the mere averments in the self serving affidavits or counter affidavits of the parties. It must be left to be evaluated and determined by expert body. The principal claim of the petitioners therefore fails and is rejected.

The prosecution alleged that in pursuance of the conspiracy and in furtherance of their common intention they committed murder of one Malan on or about 29.11.1975, while accused 1 and 6 were tried for three murders of two young girls and a women alleged to have been committed them and the approver P.W. 1 committed three murders. The Sessions Judge found that the evidence against accused 1 to 4 was not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C., and acquitted accused 7 and convicted accused 1 alone. Accused 5 and 6 filed Criminal Appeal No. 288 of 1980 respectively against their conviction and sentence awarded to them. The High Court allowed the appeal of accused 1, and set aside his conviction and the sentence awarded by the trial court under section302 read with Section 34 I P.C. and acquitted him. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the charge under section 120B I. P. C. was framed against four named persons who had been arrayed as accused 1 in respect of the murder of Malan, and that in view of the acquittal of all the seven accused by the Trial Court of charge No. 1 framed under Section 302 readwith Section 34 IPC, no appeal against their acquittal had been filed in the High Court and also the fact that accused 5 was not a party to charge No 4 which was framed only against accused 2,3,4 and 7. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will executed by her husband in favour of the respondent. The deed recited that the testator had bequeathed in favour Of the appellant half share in items 1 and 2 to the extent of Rs. 10,320 as gift with the express stipulation that the survivor of the legatees should take the whole of the bequest by survivorship. The appellant claimed a decree for possession against the respondent on the ground that she was entitled only to a life interest in items I and 2. Held, that the will did not purport to meet by anticipation the main objections which were likely to be raised to the competence of the appellant to make a will in regard to the properties covered by it. The evidence showed that the executant had taken a prominent part in bringing about the execution of the will. It was not easy to accept this part of the appel lant 's case that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the Will and put her signature on it when she was in a sound disposing state of mind. The High Court was, therefore, right in holding that the appellant had failed to prove the due and valid execution of tile will. Peri cialingam, J. The appeal must be dismissed. It is well settled that where there is proof of signature, everything else is implied till the contrary is proved; and evidence of the testator having been read over to the testator or of instructions having been given is not necessary. In the present case the appellant 's contention was that the execution was vitiated by suspicious circumstances as it had not been satisfactorily removed by the testatrix before she could be examined in support of his contention that the Will was not proved to be the last will and testament of the departed testator. The onus was heavy on him to remove all clouds and satisfy the conscience of the court that the instrument propounded was the last one of the propounder 's mind and his signature as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour o the propounder.

The appellants were selling Arcons known as "Cinema Arc Disputes" manufactured by the appellant company. The Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal, the final departmental authority under the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 had allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbons manufactured by it could be covered by the entry under consideration. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the goods under consideration were covered by Entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule of the Andhra pradesh General Sales tax Act, and that the High Court had rightly held that such arc carbon are covered by item No.4 of the first schedule to the Mysore Sales Tax, Act,1957. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience or effectiveness of something else". Other meanings given there are: "supplementary or secondary to something of greater or primary importance"; "any of several mechanical devices that assist in operating or controlling the tone resources of an organ." [564C D] The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that the main use of the arc car bons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by us, is evident from the fact that the appellants are known as 'cinema are carboons ' in the market. The entry No. 3 occurs in a schedule in which descriptions of goods to be taxed indicate that the expression "required for use there with" has been employed for equipment or accessories connected with the main purpose. For instance, in entry No 5 the expression occurs at the end as follows; "Photographic and other cameras and enlargers, films and plates, paper and cloth and other parts and accessories required for use therewith". Apparently, the deciding factor is the predominant or ordinary purpose or use. It is not enough to show that the article can be put to other uses also. [564D E] The High Court rightly held in favour of the appellant.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 in exercise of its powers conferred by Section 15 of the (67 of 1957) read with Rule 21 of the Rules framed thereunder. The Act was passed in the year 1957 by Parliament to provide for the regulation of mines and development of minerals under the control of the Union and it was made applicable to the whole of India. Under Section 3A of the Act, the word 'minerals ' is defined as including all minerals except mineral oils. Clause (e) of the said section defines minor minerals as building stones, gravel, ordinary clay, ordinary sand other than sand used for prescribed purposes and any other mineral which the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, declare to be a minor mineral. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the State Government had to be used only for mineral development and could not be used for any other purpose. According to him the Act had been passed for purposes of regulation and development and development in respect of minerals. It is contended that under entry 50 of list II of 7th schedule to the Consti tution, the tax recovered by State Government has to be utilised only for minerals and not for other purposes sanctioned by law. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The levy in question is unreasonably heavy and has been imposed in an arbitrary manner.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village at a meeting held on June 27, 1957. According to the usage of the temple the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meet of the members of his Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 1 of 1925. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the appellant was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant 's suit was barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the custom of the Temple the trustees had been elected for one year and that the appointment had to be made from the disciples of the deceased mahant if he left any, and failing disciples, any one of his spiritual kindred. HELD: (i) The term "succession" in section 6 (9) includes even such cases. But the election to the office of trustee in the present case was for a fixed period of two years and not for life. It is, therefore, difficult to hold that the office or the office which the appellant is hereditary within the mean ing of section6(9). [445 B] (ii) The word "succcession ' in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another" [427 C D] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , followed.

The deceased was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). The younger brother of the deceased, Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 p.m. On hearing the shout of his deceased brother crying "younger", he was running after stabbing me with knife, "catch him" and saw the accused Damodaran running ahead of the accused Karunakaran. He also saw two persons running ahead from the place where they were running ahead. He further saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1) and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3). He ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sleeping and fell down on the southern side of a sluice. When he went near him he was already dead. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and Pandurangam was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries two of which he described as incised and four as punctured, two more incised wounds and the remaining one as a vertical wound. These were on the left upper arm, left arm on the right side of epigastrium, on the back of the anterior axillary line, on an inter axillaries, on right side, of the epighatrium and on the outer side of it. The deceased was also sleeping on the eastern parapet of the sluices of the north Boothagudi channel, which was shown at No. 5 in the said site plan. On the hearing a noise to the effect "youounger brother", the accused was taken up for trial. The two accused were charged under section 120B read with sections 302 and 109 IPC as well as under section 302/34 IPC. The case against the first accused was referred to the High Court as usual and the accused also preferred appeals against their conviction and sentence. The High Court acquitted the second accused, but convicted the appellant on the sole testimony of PW 4 "corroborated by the contents of exhibit P1 (FIR). The High court further held that "the evidence of PW4" was not corroborated by the facts of the FIR. On appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the High court erred in convicting the second appellant on his sole testimony as he implicated the second respondent and Tharnizasan in the case of murder of Viswanatham". Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of the sole eye witness (PW 4) was not wholly corroborated by contents of the F.I.R. [712B] 2. It is difficult to accept this explanation of PW 5 that he had any witnesses and that he "did not tell about them due to excitement". It is, therefore, a case where conviction of the second defendant depends on the evidence of a single witness.

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. Amarchand died on July 7, 1949. Thereafter the partnership was carried on by Mangaldas and Hiralal up to November 30, 1949, and on December 1, 1949 Ramesh son of Amarchand who had by then qualified as a solicitor joined the firm as the third partner. After the death of Amar Chand the arrangement between the various partners in regard to the realisations of the old outstandings was that in respect of the work done up to the death Of Amarchand the realises were to be divided amongst Amarchand, Mangaldas, Hiralal and Ramesh. The firm kept its accounts on cash basis. For the five assessment years 1950 51 to 1954 55 the following amounts were received : Rs. 37,847/ . As 43,162/ , Rs. 34,899/ . Rs. 13,402/ and Rs. 32,523/ by the heirs and legal representatives of Amarachand out of thestandings. The Income tax Officer sought to tax these realisations. For those assessment years the respondents claimed that the amounts were not the income of the Hindu undivided family but merely represented inheritance or realisations or realisable of the assets of Amarichand. Held, that the words "if he had not died" mean that irrespective of the date of receipt of income receivable by a person, if the income is received by his heirs and Legal representatives after his death they are liable for payment of the tax just as the deceased would have been liable when the income was received had he been living. The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three sub sections of section 24B and cannot be extended further than the liability for the income received in the previous year. In re Sreemati Usharani Shoudhurani, (1938) 22 Tax Cases 10, Ellis C. Reid vs Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay City, , referred to.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All of them were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. On January 19, 1969 leaders of all political parties in the Legislature of the State appeared to have met and reached the decision that to Implement what are called Telengana Safeguards ', the following measures should be taken : "All non domicile persons who have been appointed either directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra Pra Pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 for domiciles of Telengna region will be immediately relieved from service. The posts so rendered vacant will be filled by qualified candidates possessing domicile qualifications and in cases where such candidates are not available the posts shall be left unfilled till qualified domicile candidates become available. Action on these supernumerary posts were to be treated as temporary addition to the strength of the office concerned and were to he adjusted against future vacancies in corresponding posts as they arose. The action was based upon section 3 of the Public Employment Act, 1957 (44 of 1957) which was an Act of Parliament made in pursuance of cl. (3) of article 16 of the Constitution making special provision for requirement as to residence and brought into force on March 21, 1959. Section 3 of that Act gave power to make rules in respect of certain classes of employment in certain areas. It provided that power to frame rules in regard to appointments to (a) any subordinate service or post under the State Government of Andhra Pradesh or any requirement as regards residence within that State or Union territory prior to such appointment, shall be made by notification in the Official Gazette, make rules prescribing, in regard, among others, the conditions subject to which a person shall not be eligible for appointment to a post within the Telenganana area under the state Government of A. P. O.Ms. 36, G.A. (SR) Department dated January 21, 1969 relieving before February 28, 1969 all non domicile employees appointed on or after November 1, 1956 to certain categories of posts reserved for domicics of Telangana region will he immediately relieved of from service; and (b) in the case of posts in the Secretariat Departments and Offices of the Heads of Departments of the Government of the A.P. Government then passed an order relieving before Feb 28,1969 all non resident persons appointed on November 1 1956 to some categories of post reserved for domicile of Telongana region would be immediately relieve from service, and by creating supernumerary posts, if necessary. The Government of India then passed orders (G.O.Ms 36,G.A.) relieving the petitioners before February 27, 1969, all non permanent vacancies were to been filled by direct requirement; but the action was challenged on section 3 Of the Act as ultra vires the Constitution. Held: (i) The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended use given to it by the definition of that word article 12. The second clause then specifies a prohibition against discrimination only on the grounds of religion, race, sex, descent, place of birth, residence or any of them. The intention here is make every office or employment open and available to every citizen, and inter alia to make offices or employment in one part India open to citizens in all other parts of India. (ii) The claim for supremacy of Parliament is misconceived. Par liament in this case as in other matters, is supreme only in so far as the Constitution makes it. Where the Constitution does not concede supremacy, Parliament must act within its appointed functions and not transgress them. What the Constitution says is a matter for, construction of the language of the constitution.

The appellant was a postman attached to the Bulandshahr post office. At the time of search, the appellant who happens to be a trade union official, was not in Bulandshahr but was away on leave at Delhi in connection with a postal conference. The articles were found in an almirah and the key of which was produced by the appellant 's father. The appellant ' defence in all these cases was that there were two factions in the Bulandshahr Post office and that these articles were planted by the opposite party. According to him, the planting must have occurred in the Kotwali when the Sub Inspector purported to make a list of the articles seized from the house in which the appellant lives. The prosecution case was that these documents were found at an almirah of the house and that they were in his exclusive possession. Held, that though the locked almirah was not In the exclusive possession of the appellant, these articles could be said to have secreted them from the mere fact that they had been found in the almirah which was said to had been in his separate possession along with his father because he had the opportunity to get at the articles and then infer that he must have utilized the opportunity and was therefore in their exclusive possession would be arguing in a circle. The fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be in course of transmission. It is common experience that delivery of postal articles is now and again delayed for a considerable length of time may be through accident or through the negligence of the postal employees.

The appellants, who were Sarpanch and the Sarpanch of a Gram Panchayat, filed a complaint before the Nyaya Panchayat against the five appellants. The complaint was adjourned to December 25, 1963. On October 11, 1963, the Sarpanch refused to take it on the ground that the complainant had been abused and he be laboured and his property worth Rs. 40/ damaged. The complainant and the accused were present. The statements of the complainant and his witnesses were recorded on oath. The appellants denied having knowledge of the interim stay order passed by the High Court. The High Court held that the Sarpanch was not proper and that the matter should file a proper affidavit in support of his allegations, though the Sarpanch had admitted in his deposition that he had to authority to tell Mahabir that his affidavit was not correct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court erred in holding that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit at all and that no such application was made after the proceedings on that date had commenced and evidence taken. HELD : (i) The High court did not appreciate that the So called affidavit was filed by the Sarpanch before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Panchachas to enquire from the S.D.M. about the filing of the application before him.

The appellant was tried along with others for the murder of a person who was sleeping in his cattle shed. The prosecution case was that due to enmity, the appellant caused injuries to Sheo Sahai and asked him to go to the Police Station, Ekdil, nine miles away and lodged a report. He delivered the sword which had been found by the Serologist to be stained with human blood. The appellant was taken in custody and as a result of investigation was sent up for trial. The Sessions Judge believed Ujagar Singh 's statement about the appellant 's confessing to him that he had murdered Sheo Sahai, that he did commit the murder. On appeal the High Court acquitted the appellant on the ground that it was inadmissible in evidence as its contents amounted to a confession of the offence by the appellant made to a Police Officer and that the evidence relied upon by the High court was insufficient to establish that the appellant had murdered the deceased. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The extra judicial confession of an accused to Ujagar Singh finds ample support from the facts that the accused did purchase a sword day before, that very sword was found to be connected with human Blood shortly after the murder and that sword was handed over by the accused himself to the police Officer at the Police station. [205 C] (ii) The evidence of the appellant having enmity with Sheo Sahai came to support Ujagar Singh, P.W.

The appellants challenged the validity of the electoral roll, the calendar of events and the declaration of results of election. The High Court dismissed the petition holding (i) that respondent No. 2 had asked petitioner No. S to appear before him on October 30, 1978 and that as he did not produce any evidence in support of his claim, his application was dismissed; (ii) that none of the persons mentioned in Annexure P 7 preferred any claim before respondent No 2 on October 20, 1978 or on any other sub sequent date; and (iii) that the petitioners were not entitled to any relief under Article 226 of the Constitution on account of the inordinate delay involved in the presentation of the writ petition. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of the High Court under Article226 of the constitution to issue an appropriate writ is discretionary and if the High court finds that there is not satisfactory explanation far the inordinate time, it may reject the petition if it finds that the issue of Writ will lead to public inconvenience and interference with rights of others. [495E F] 2. The question whether in a given case the delay involved is such that it dissentients a person to relief under article 226 is a matter within the discretion of the high Court which as in all matters of discretion has to exercise it judiciously and reasonably having regard to the surrounding circumstances. [498A B] 3. The petitioners were entitled to the issue prayed for as of right and the delay in filing the petition should have been ignored.

The respondent company and its directors were prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) of the Companies Act, 1913 for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of that Act. The High Court upheld the acquittal of the directors by the Presidency Magistrate. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the principle accepted by this Court in the State of Bombay vs Bandhan Ram Bhandani & Ors., ; , that a company or its directors in a prosecution under section 32 and section 133 of the 1913 Act could not in defence to such prosecution rely upon their failure to call the general body meeting as a defence to the prosecution; (ii) the principles accepted by the Supreme Court in The State of Madras vs Bandan Ram Bhandarani & Anr., ; and that a person charged with an offence cannot rely on his default as an answer to the charge and so, if he was responsible for not calling the general meeting, he could not be heard to say in defence; (iii) the view taken by this court in the instant case was contrary to the one taken earlier by a Judge of that High Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balance sheets and profit & loss account is a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. If no general body meets any one meeting and omit to lay the balance Sheet and profit or loss account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable udder aforesaid provisions. [419 C] 2. The words "were so laid" make the filing of copies of those balance sheets or the profit and losses account which are laid before a general body and for not sending a statement of the fact that the balancesheet was not adopted. It is possible to conceive of the law providing that the provisions of section 134 were not complied with even then, the persons concerned would be liable for punishment for that default. [416 C] 3. The court there observed that this is not a case where an accused person relies on his failure and pleads his innocence. What he says is, I may have committed an offence, but the offence that I have committed is not the one with which I am charged. On the facts proved by the prosecution an offence is not disclosed under section 134(4). A different offence might have been committed either under section 76(2) or under section 133(1)(3). It is interesting to note that it was argued in Park vs Lawton (supra) that the principle laid down in Park v Lawton, is based on section 36(it is a mistake for section 26 of the English Act, which in its scheme and terms is entirely different from the section with which they (the Bombay High Court) were concerned. [414 D E] 4.

The respondent and 49 other persons were charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by them in the course of their raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum, and they were convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprison ment by the Special Court to which the case was sent for trial by the Governor of West Bengal by a notification dated 26th January 1950 in exercise of the powers conferred by section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Ordinance, 1949. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special Judge had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5 (1) was not applicable to the case because section 5 of the Act was not made applicable to it. Held, that the classification implied in this part of the sub section has no reference to, and is not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but is concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" or "cl classes of cases". The word "category of offences " in article 14 does not mean the "legal precepts which are actually recognised and applied in the tribunals of a given time and place" but "the more general body of doctrine and tradition from which those precepts are chiefly drawn, and by which they criticise them. It is the function of the legislature alone, headed by the Government of the day to determine what is for the good of the people and substitute their individual opinions for that of the government of the date, or that they may usurp the functions of the Legislature. The fact that it gives unre strained power to the State Government to select in any way it likes the particular cases or offences which should go to a Special Tribunal and withdraw in such cases the protec tion which the accused normally enjoy under the criminal law of the country is on the face of it discriminatory. It may be that this power is controlled by the necessity for making a proper classifi cation which is guided by the preamble in the sense that the classify must have a rational relation to the object of the legislation as recited in the preamble. The classification implied, in this sub section is not violative of article 14 of the Constitu tion and is therefore bad. It matters not to me, nor indeed to them and their families and friends whether this be done in good faith, whether it be done for the convenience of Government, whether the process can be scientifically classified or labelled, or whether it is an experiment in speedier trials made for the purpose of being tried by a Special Court. The Act itself is not unconstitutional as being opposed to equality before the law and the equal protection of the laws guaranteed under article 14.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd. (the Company) were engaged in the manufacture of paper on a very large scale. These two Paper Mills were, therefore, both of very recent origin compared with the Company. The strength of their labour force and the annual production was also very mueh lower. Even the profits earned were much smaller. On these facts, the Tribunal held that it would not be proper to compare the wage structure for these Paper Mills with that of the Company, and that there was no justification for departing from the figure of Rs. 95 which is the average minimum wage payable by those industries (1) [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 678. The Tribunal also took into account the minimum wages being paid by other Paper Mills situated outside the region and thereafter recorded its own decision in the following words : "The conclusion that flows from these figures is that the lowest paid worker in the Paper Mill at the then existing Price Index was Rs. 93 7 0; in the Cement Factory Rs. 96.88, in the Steel Plant Rs. 97.84 nP. In appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The Tribunal committed no error of law requiring interference by this Court in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of the parties and in holding that there is marked variation in the Price Index and the Labour 's Case (1)[1963] Suppl. 673), followed.

The appellant was carrying on a business as partners from the beginning of Samvat 1994 (March 1, 1937) in which year it was replaced by the present Act. The firm consisted of Nagjee, Narayanjee and Manecklal who were members of the original family. In the deed of 1918 the earlier partnership deed of April 4, 1902 was revoked and the affairs of the firm were to be regulated and governed by the new deed. Under the terms and conditions of the revo ked deed the business was carried on by two independent firms for the purpose of carrying on the business as a Partners from the end of the previous year and the business which had been charged under the Act of 1918, was discontinued in 1937. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income tax Appellate Tribunal held that the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal by the assessee, Held: (i) Under section 25 (4), a mere change in the constitution of the partnership does not necessarily bring into existence a new assessable unit or a distinct assessable entity and in such a case there is no devolution of the business of the old firm as a whole; (ii) under the Indian Incometax Act, 1918, a firm is by section 3 made a unit or assessment, but this personality does not make the firm a person in every sense of the word. The first sub section deals with a change in constitution of a firm or where a firm has been newly constituted and the second sub section where there is a succession to the person (which includes a firm) (1) (2) [1956] S.C.R. 969, followed. (iii) under section 26(2), a case of succession was not to be found where there was a mere discontinuance of the 859 business before 1948 or a succession not amounting to a mere alteration in the Constitution of the partner between 1939 and 1948 that the appellants can be denied the benefit of section 25. The fact that an express agreement to carry on the partnership business in partnership was made (for which see the third recital in the preamble) further indicates that the agreement to that effect in the instrument of December 6, 1918 was no longer subsisting did not affect the questions in this case because, as a result of the splitting up there was discontinuance of a original business at the date of the partition and on such discontinuance the family became entitled to relief under s.25 (4) and section 26 (2). The fact of the use of the words "unless there has been a succession by virtue of which the provisions of sub section (4)(4) have been rendered applicable.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations, 1960 were replaced by the Life Insurance Corpora tion (Emergency Provisions) Ordi nance, 1956 on January 19, 1956. The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial political matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of the Government was not good in this country. The appellants, who were members of the Bar Association, sent a letter addressed to the Chief Justice of Punjab and Haryana High Court, the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Chief Jus tice of Punjab, the Prime Minister. In that letter they said that the Honble Judge during his entire stay in his tour deliberately showed the bent of his mind towards commu nism while exchanging view on various matters. The appellant also expressed his desire to see Comrade Dharam Singh a member of the Marxist Communist Party at his residence before Smt. Chandrawati. During his stay in the rest house he also discussed the teachers agitation and individual position of various political leaders in the State. He also enquired all about Shri Sohan Lal a leader of the teacher 's movement in the States. The letter was addressed to, the President. In reply the appellant stated that the contents of the letter were correct. It was further stated that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon"ble Judge or this Hon ' ble Court or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of the learned Judge or of the Hon ble Court in any way the confidence of the people in the administration of justice. The High Court did not take any action against two persons on the letter written by five members of Bar Association of Charkhi Dadri. Each of the appellants affirmed an affidavit in this pattern. It is an article of faith with the deponent that dignity and respect of all Courts and of all Judges and particularly of the High Court must be maintained for, amongst other reasons, on that depends the orderly function ing of the society as also prestige of profession to which the deponent has the honour to belong. The deponent has been taught to believe that a Judge ought always to steer clear of all avoidable controversial matters. It will not be correct and proper for any Judge to accept the invitation and hospitality of any busi ness or commercial organisation or of any political party or of a club or organisation run on sectarian, communal parochial lines. Invitations by the Bar Associa tion or social invitations naturally stand on a different footing and no one will find an exception to any Judge attending a social function. Judges are by reason of their office and nature of work expected not to get involved in controversial matter, or to concern themselves with political issues or policies under taken by political parties as a part of their political programme.

The respondent, a company registered under section 26 of the Indian Companies Act 1913, was carrying on business as it was "tendering advice to all businessmen and traders". The primary objects of the Federation as given in the Memorandum of Association are (a) To promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade; (b) to secure the interest of the country. It is predominantly a charitable organisation and not a professional one. It was then contended that the activities of the respondent were carried on in the premises in question amounted to "work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary" to trade or business in general within the latter part of the definition of "commercial establishment". This contention was negatived by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the activity of the appellant Federation carried on activities in the Premises in question amounts to "business" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act and (ii) the activities were carried out in the nature of material services within the wider definition of 'industry '. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of this Federation is one of general utility; the only source of its income is from subscriptions. The occasional exhibitions orIndore visited by it are activities which are only incidental or subsidiary to the primary charitable object of the association. [350 C] 2.1 In R. K.

The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Trivikram Narain Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. The district of Monaras was formerly part of Oudh territory. By a Treaty between the East India Company Nawab Asfuddaula in or about the year 1775, the province of Benares was ceded to the British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhittery in perpetuity to Babu Ausan Singh. It appears that in 1796 there were some disputes between Babu Auusan and the Zamindars in the District and the matter was referred by the Collector of Benarsingh to the Board of Revenue in Calcutta. The amount of pension was determined at Rs. 36,322/8/ . On appeal the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the sum of Rs.36,396/ was chargeable to tax under the Indian Income tax Act as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was fixed with respect to the quantum of rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the pension. The source of this pension was a liability undertaken by the Government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate sources of the income were not land or rent collections from land, it was difficult to hold that the receipt of the assessee was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of the Income tax. The High Court held that from the language of the letter of July 7, 1837, Babu Har Narain Singh and his successors were granted in perpetuity a right to one fourth of the land revenue collections themselves and not merely a right of receiving u sum of money calculated on that basis. On appeal by certificate: HELD : (i) The source and character of the receipt are, therefore, altered when a part of the agricultural income of the trust is appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration, and that is so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the value of the disputed title of the appellant 's predecessor in 1837. [707 C] (ii) The allowance is revenue income and not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. Therefore, the allowance is Revenue income and cannot be held to be derived from land within the ambit of section 2(1)(a) of Income tax, 1922. [700 F G] State of Uttar Pradesh vs Kunwar Sri Trivkram Narayan Singh, ; , followed.

The Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Tourism Development Corporation and some other private operators filed these appeals by special leave of this Court under Article 136 of the Constitution. The main question for consideration in these appeals was whether the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this court in Sher Singh 's case and that the true position was that on a correct interpretation of the proviso to section 63(7), the preference became operative only if other things were equal. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Karnataka State Transport Corporation Act, 1976 is constitutionally valid and the appellants who did not get a certificate of approval from the Central Government, because of the rule of preference contained in proviso to Section 63(1) of the Act, the proper course for this Court was to set aside the orders of the State Appellate Tribunal, and the Division Bench directed the State Road Appellate Tribunal to hear the appeals in the light of what we have said. [1015C] 2. The very idea that a Tribunal created by a statute for the purpose of considering rival claims and granting permits on merits should be compelled to give peference to persons securing the approval of the executive Government, appears to us to be arbitrary and unreasonable. To the extent that it goes, the clause pre empts the decision in Sher Sing Singh ' 's Case in relation to section 47(1 H) applies mutatis mutandis to the preference contemplated by the proviso, to Section63(7). Since the State transport Appellate Tribunal & the High court have failed to consider the merits of the claims of the Karnataka state Road Transport Corpora tion and the private operators who did neither get a Certificate of approval of from the Government, the appropriate course for the appellants was to be set aside. [109E F] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to. In the instant case, it is difficult to agree with the interpretation of Karnataka High Court having regard to the definitions of "Transport Vehicle" and "motor car" contained in Section 2(29 A) and section 2(16) respectively. [ 1016F] 3.

The respondent purchased, by a registered instrument dated October 5, 1956, the business carried on by one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company. The assessee paid some amounts towards sales tax thus determined but there remained some arrears of sales tax i.e., Rs. 3836 4 0 for 1948 49, and Rs. 1218 1 9 for 1949 50 The Sales Tax authorities attempted to recover the arrears of tax from the respondent as the purchaser of the said business. The respondent 6 63 denied liability to pay sales tax but his contention was over ruled by the Deputy Commercial Tax Officer. The appellant then moved the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the orders of the Commercial Tax officer and the Board of Revenue. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that Rule 21 A was ultra vires of the rule making power of the State Government under section 19(1) and (2) of the Act. Bihar, , Chattaram vs C., I. T. Bihar and Chattamuram vs Commissioner of Inland Revenue, A. 1. R. , referred to.

The plaintiff entered service in the Gondal State in 1927 as a jailor. The Gondal state merged with the United States of Saurashtra. On March 6, 1953, he was suspended and at that time he was acting as Accountant at Rajkot Central Jail. On April 7, 1954, he had committed certain acts of mis appropriation of food stuffs meant for prisoners maltreatment of prisoners and acceptance of illegal gratification from them. The plaintiff filed a written statement on September 4, 1954 and an enquiry was held by the Enquiry Officer who made a report and on or about January 7, 1955, the following notice was issued to him calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service "To Shri Bhaishanker A. Joshi, Accountant, Rajkot Central Prison (Under suspension) Charges framed against you under this office No. C/ 14 dated 27 3 54 and in particular the charges of having accepted illegal gratification by prisoner Ratilal Jivan had been established to the satisfaction of Government. You are hereby asked to showcause why the punishment of dismissal from service should not he inflicted upon you. " The plaintiff failed before the Civil Judge, Rajkot, but on appeal succeeded before the District Judge, Central Saurashtra, inasmuch as he declared order dated February 2/4, 1955 illegal and void. The High Court held that there had been a breach of article 311(2) of the Constitution as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy of the report of the enquiry held against the plaintiff. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the plaintiff with a copy Of the report amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311 (2) and consequently he had not been given reasonable opportunity within the meaning of article 31(2).

The appellants ' colliery owners filed a suit for the recovery of certain quantity of coal from their colliery. The trial court held that article 48 of the Limitation Act applied to the suit and that the appellant had failed to prove that they had knowledge of the said encroachment only within three years thereof. On appeal, the High Court accepted the finding of fact on the question of knowledge. Held, further, that a map referred to in a lease should be treated as incorporated in the lease deed and as forming part of the document, the suit was within time. It is the obligation of the plaintiff to satisfy the court that his action is not barred by lapse of time. The burden of proof may shift to the defendant. But to say that no duty is cast upon the plaintiff even to allege the date when they had know of the defendant 's possession of the converted property and that he has to prove the necessary facts. In the present case, the onus of proof in the former sense was on the respondents. But the question was whether the suit Was barred by limitation. Held further, also, that the burden of proving knowledge on the part of a party who comes to court to get a decision on the existence of certain facts which he asserts. That burden is constant throughout the trial; but the burden to prove in the sense of adducing evidence shifts from time to time having regard to the evidence adduced by one party or the other or the presumption of fact or law raised in favour of one or the others.

The appellant, a saw mill in the State of Kerala, was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It was alleged that on June 21, 1958, Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. Sankaran gave an explanation the same day denying the allegations of fact made against him though he admitted that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. On July 8, 1958 Sankaran again wrote to the appellant to hold the inquiry as early as possible. On August 9, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental enquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21. 1958 but there was no evidence to prove what had actually happened. It further held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the workman but subsequently departmental proceedings were dropped and action was taken under r, 18(b) of Standing Orders. The Tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under rule 18 (a) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer, the Secretary and other members of the staff whose evidence would have been of more value had not been produced and no explanation had been given why they were not produced. The tribunal therefore held that on the facts it could not come to its conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the Mill and abused or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or the other officers. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to termination of service even under a rule like 18(A). The employer could defend the actions under r . 18(c) by leading evidence before the Tribunal to show that there was in fact misconduct and therefore the action was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of the power under that rule. (ii) Even if the inquiry was not held by the appellant and action taken thereunder, it is now well settled that the employer could dismiss the action under r ' 18(d).

The appellants were the owners of a theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and Garaquii on the one hand and Messrs. Filmistan Distributors (India) Private Ltd., hereinafter called "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 in the Court of Small Causes Ahmedabad against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960, to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By order dated December 31, 1960 the suit was disposed of as compromised. It was inter alia agreed that Raval and Earaqua were bound and liable to allow Filmistans to exercise their "exhibition rights" in the Theatre; that Raval, their servants and agents were not to have any right to exhibit any picture in contravention of the terms and condi tions of the agreement. The trial Judge passed an order disallowing the objection raised by the appellants. The revision application against that order was dismissed in limine by the High Court. When the case reached hearing and the evidence of a representative of Filmistna was being recorded, counsel for the defendants asked in cross examination the question whether the "agreement between the plaintiff and the defendant Nos. 5 and 6 were barred on principles of res judicata" from agitating the question that the said document dated November 1, 1954 as confirmed by their letter dated January 31, 1955 and further confirmed by document dated December l, 1960 was not a lease; and that in any event the suit No 149 of 1961 was for declaration of the rights of Films to exhibit cinematograph films, in view of section 92 of the Evidence Act. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the document could be permitted to 'be put to the witnesses for Filmisthan; and (ii) that the consent decree in suit No, 149 of 1953 had not decided that the agreement was of the nature Of a lease. HELD : (i). The order passed by the trial court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [446 E] (ii). A consent decree accord ing to the decisions of this Court, does not operate as res judicata, because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the parties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as Res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court : the terms of section II of the Code leave no scope for a contrary view. [441 G] (iii) The expression "case" is not limited in its import to the entirety of the matter in dispute in an action. This Court observed in Major section Khanna vs Brig. F. J. Dillon, [1893] 1 K.B.D. 426, that the expression " case" is a word of comprehensive import and includes a civil proceeding and is not restricted by anything contained in section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code to the extent to which the Court, viz., the trial Court in the instant case, proposed to go into that question and allow the whole question, that was closed once for all by consent decree of December 1.

The respondent, a pilot Officer was granted a permanent commission in the Indian Air Force and was, therefore, inval idated from I.A.F. The Government of India issued a scheme for the benefit of ex military officials. The State of Uttar Pradesh also adopted the same scheme. Under that scheme the ex military official officials were appointed on contract basis for a fixed term which could be extended from time to time subject to the suitability of the official concerned but not beyond 58 years of age. Pursuant to the said scheme the State Government of Uttar pradesh appointed the respondent as Secretary, Zila Sainik Board, Unnao on 20th August, 1979. Paragraph 2 of the order of appointment issued on 20.8.1979 provided that the appointment shah be on contract for a period of one 241 year w.e.f. the date of assumption if it is not terminated earlier by giving a one month 's notice by the Hon 'ble Gover or on paying one month"s salary in lieu thereof or by giving one month "s notice, by the Officer. " The respondent was required to furnish his acceptance of the terms and conditions contained in the said order includ ing the above term relating to the period of appointment and on his accepting the terms of conditions he was appointed as Secretary in the District Soldiers Board in the district of UnnaOo in the State of U.P. The said term was extended retrospectively, first upto 20th of August, 1985 by an order dated 1st June 1983. Again the term was extend ed upto 30th August 1985 by another order dated 31st March, 1983. All these orders of exten sion were couched almost in the same language. The relevant part of the last such orders, namely, the order dated Ist June, 1983, read as follows: "Sir, With reference to your letter No. 1020/Sa. A.D.M./141, Dated 31.3.1982 on the above subject I am directed to say that the terms Of the officers mentioned under para 2 who were appointed w.f .the date mentioned in para 4 (has expired). The Governor is pleased to accord his sanction to extend the period upto the period mentioned under Para 5 subject to t he condi tion that their service tenure shall expire on completion of 58 years in case the same is completed earlier during the extended period. No. Name and Date of Recommen tation of relevant conditions of service to be obtained from these officers must be submitted to the Government at an early date. " It was thus seen that the respondent was employed only under a contract which specified the term of his appointment which extended only upto 30 th August,1985. Since it is admitted that no order of extension had been sanctioned by the Governor beyond 30th of 885, the respondent, was entitled to the salary and allowances due to him till 30th September, 1985 if the order terminating service served on him on 29th March, 1985 was found to be an invalid one.
