The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was appointed under Article 124 and under Article 217 of the Constitution. The Chief Justice of India, in exercise of his executive power, had to act judicially in the exercise of any power which is, or which in good faith he believes to be, given to him by law. The President, therefore, being the authority competent to appoint and to remove a Judge from his office, issued an order under his hand and seal after consultation with the Chief Justice, appointed a Judge by warrant under his Hand and seal for the purpose of carrying out the duties of a Judge. The appellant challenged the validity of the said order before the High Court which dismissed the same on the ground that it was not competent to remove him from his post except by an order of the President passed after an address by both Houses of Parliament in the manner provided under Article 122(4) and (5) of the Constitu tion. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the Judge of a High Court is a constitutional functionary and there is no employer and employee relationship or master and servant relationship between the Judge and the President of India and for that reason the Central Government or the State Government there isno authority to remove the Judge from 'his office by the executive except by taking recourse to procedure of impeachment as envisaged in Article 124(4), clauses (4) & (5). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The President has not been given the sole power or the exclusive power to remove any Judge either of the High Courts and the Supreme court within the purview of the Act for the pur pose of grant of previous sanction for prosecution which is a condition precedent for cognizance of an offence punhable under that Act. [226B] 1.2 The President is given the power to appoint the Judges of the Court as well as of the Chief justice by warrant and seal and similarly even after passing of an address, both Houses have been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. [227C D] 1:3 The President can appoint the judges of the high Courts as well of the Judges. [228D E] 2.1 In the instant case, the Judge is a Constitutional functionary and has been observed by this Court in Shamsher Singh & Anr. vs State of Punjab, ; , that for the purposes of grant ing sanction under Section 6 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947, he must be treated to be outside the purview o the Act since this special enactment was not enacted to cover that category of public servants inspite of the wide definition of 'public servant ' in the Act. The scheme of the , is that a public servant who commits the offence of criminal misconduct, as defined in the seven clauses of Sub section (1) of Section 5 can be punished in accordance with sub section (2) of section 5 after investigation of the offence in the way prescribed and with the previous sanction of the competent authority obtained under Section6 of the . [228G H; 228A] 1 :3 The power to punish a High Judge, if one may so describe it, is to be found only in Article 2 read with article 124(5) and that the President could be the proper authority under clause (c) of Article 124 of the constitution.

The appellant was a member of a Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were the former was declared elected. The respondent challenged the validity of the order of the High Court rejecting his prayer to be declared elected, on various grounds. At the hearing of the petition by the Election Tribunal, however, he challenged the election only on the ground that Abhiman Pada was a Member of the Saha caste and not a member thereof. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The appellant was not a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to the smaller caste group of Sahas. He must be held to belong lo the Scheduled Caste specified in item 40. [390 E] (ii) The Tribunal was wrong in considering the Sahas as an independent caste. [391 C] (iii) The expression "excluding" denoted that the Saha ' contemplated would, but for this word had come within the Sunri caste. It is legitimate to think that when a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste. the other must be a caste; it follows that when the item excluded Sahas from Sunris, since Sunri was a caste group, Saha must equally be another caste group. [392 E G] (iv) The finding that Sahas were a 'a group within the ' Sunri Caste ' is irrelevant as a test for applying item 40 unless it is shown that it indicated a smaller caste Group of Sunris. It was not necessary that such part must necessarily form a sub caste. The Tribunal, therefore, rightly held that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondent belonged to a smaller community group of ' Sahas and was thereby excluded from the Scheduled Castes specified in Item 40 for he said "these Saha families, within the fold of Sunri castes".

The appellant was carrying on a business in Bombay under the name and style of Associated Commercial Enterprises, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one, the rent being Rs. 215. It was agreed to be paid back on the appellant 's return to India. The complainant and his wife were leaving the flat, the man who masqueraded as the complain ant 's brother threw off his disguise and disclosed his identity. The police party, who were down below ready for the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement was tween the complainant and the appellant. The appellant was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 for receiving a pugree of Rs 29,500 and he was further charged under s 19(2) of that Act for receiving the said sum as a condition for the relin quishment of his tenancy. The defence of the appel lant was that he was in search of a partner to carry on his business during his intended absence, who was also to act as caretaker of his flat anal that it was in this connection and with this object in view in view that he entered into negotiations with the complain er. The prosecution case was that the accused demanded a sum of money which was later on reduced to Rs. 29, 500 as consideration for putting the complainant in vacant possession of the flat and an additional amount of Rs 2,000 for the furniture, and that the complainant agreed to pay these sums. The wife of the deceased, denied any aiding and abetting. The Presidency Magistrate who tried the case convicted him under section 19(1)(c) of 'the Act and sentenced him in view of his old age and blindness to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs 30,000. The appeal preferred by the appellant was summarily rejected on 20 2 1950. On 10 4 1950 the wife of appellant denied any aid and abetting her husband in the commission of the two offences. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the ground that what was received by the accused was by way of pugna tree, and as s.18(1), was not applicable he convicted him thereunder under section19(2). On appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant relying on the language of section 19 (1) Of the Act and this was the only point which required our consideration. Held: The section in question, is not concerned so much with what might possibly have been intended as with what has been actually said in and by the language employed. As in the present case there had been no "relinquishment" within the meaning of section19, sub cl.(1), the conviction under sub clause (2) cannot be sustained. It is set aside and the fine of RS. 30 will be refunded if it has ready been paid. The other parts of the order of the Presidency Magistrate as regards the disposal of Rs 1,000 paid by the complainant to the appellant were also held.

The workmen of Tata Consulting Engineers, at its inception was a partnership firm but subsequently the partnership was dissolved and in 1974 the undertaking became one of the divisions of Tata Sons Limited. It functions as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and does not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consists of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of 665 employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306 were. These workmen are members of the Tata Consultating Engineers ' Union. They served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. 170 The Union filed a statement before the Tribunal claiming an upward revision of the wage scales and dearness allowance and an increase from fifteen years to twenty years in the span for earning annual increments increments. It was urged that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the Union were accepted. The Tribunal rejected the demand of the union for abolishing the Efficiency Bar, but the modified terms according to the Tribunal, appeared to be on the high side inasmuch as the resulting total burden of Rs. 1.70 crores was much higher than the average profits could sustain. The particular character of the appellant, that it was a service Industry and not a manufacturing concern, was taken into account and it was observed that besides the staff staff of 306 workmen represented by the Union there were several other employees who would also have to be paid, the Tribunal considered it fair, in paragraph 23 of the award, to give a flat increase of Rs 150/ to each draughtsman and Rs. 100/ to all other workmen in their basic pay. The Industrial Tribunal took note of the elaborate scales of wages already existing in the wage structure of the appellants and decided "to modify the existing structure of scales with flat increases in each category". It also observed that the category of Draughtsmen needed a special increase. But it rejected the claim of the Unions for dearness allowance on the basis of a slab system, because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the Appellant 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. Taking into account the circumstance that besides staff of employees represented by Union there had been several other employee who would have also to be pay, the Industrial Tribunal went on to say: "I only propose to modify the new existing structure Of the scales with flats increased in each categories". The Tribunal took a note of all the relevant factors which prevailed with it in giving retrospectivity to the revised pay scales. They are considerations which cannot be ignored. Accordingly, the contention raised on behalf of the workmen against retrospectivity of the Wage scales must be rejected.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance of the said award, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said Award. This agreement was subsequently published in the Bihar Gazette as a part of the award. In spite of the awards and the agreement, the appellant paid its employees only As. 10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the payment of wages authority that the refusal of the appel lant to pay to them wages at the rate awarded in substance amounted to an illegal deduction from their wages, and on that basis they asked for an order from the authority directing the appellant to pay the said prescribed wages. The appellant raised two pleas against the respondents ' claim. It was urged before the authority that section 15 Of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. The authority rejected the appellant 's contention that the applications made by them were incompetent under section15 of the , as the rates prescribed by an award did amount to wages as defined by section 1(vi). Held, that even under the unamended definition of Wages, rates of remuneration prescribed by a award could not be included. In dealing with the question of construing the unamended definitions of the term "wages" it is essential to bear in mind the scope and character of the powers conferred on Industrial Tribunals when they deal with industrial disputes under the provisions of the Indus trial Disputes Act. It is now well settled that unlike ordinary civil courts which are bound by the terms of contract between the parties when they dealt with disputes arising between them in respect of the same terms, Industrial adjudication is not bound to uphold the terms Of contract between tho employer and the employees.

The appellant was charged under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code for forging the thumb impression of Parma, and under section 477 A with having failed to enter them in the stock book. The trial Magistrate acquitted him but convicted him under section 465 and section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. On appeal by the State to the High Court it was discovered that there was no order sanctioning the prosecution and that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure for his prosecution, that the evidence on record was insufficient to establish an offence either under section 466 or section 409, and that there having been an acquittal of the appellant by the trial Magistrate, the materials on record did not justify a reversal of that verdict by the appellate Court. Held, that sanction was required under section 198(1), as the official capacity was involved in the very act complained of as amounting to a crime; but if they do, then sanction is necessary. Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli vs The State of Bombay ([1948] L.R 75 I.A. 180) and Albert West Meads vs The King ([1947] L .R. 75 I A. 180), referred to. Held further that the acts with which the appellant was alleged could not be justified as done by virtue of his office, no sanction under s 197( 1) was necessary; and the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. Shree kantiah R. B. Gill vs The Queen ([1948) L. R 75 I .A. 185), distinguished.

The assessee was a private limited company with its registered office in the former Cochin State. It filed its incometax return showing an income of Rs. 11,872 for the assessment year 1948 49, its accounting year being the previous calendar year. The Income tax Officer determined its assessable income to be Rs. 90 representing only the profit it made in Travancore State and under section 32(1) proviso (1) of the Travancore Act he refused a deduction of Rs 79,275 shown as loss from branches situate outside the State of Travancore. The Appellate Tribunal also did not accept the submissions of the assessee and upheld the order of assessment. On an application of the assesse for the following question was referred to the High Court of Travancore Cochin: " Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the loss of Rs 27,709 arising in Cochin State could be set off against the profit of Rs., 38,998 arising in Travancore state ? and was answered in favour of the assesses. The Commissioner appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. Held: (i) The proviso to section 24(1)(a) of Travancore Act is not only prospective but also introduced an addendum or a similar addition that where the profits of the business arose in what was British India in the case of the Indian Act or what was Travancore State in the latter case in any other Indian State or British India, these losses could not by virtue of the proviso be deducted from profits made in British India or Travancore State as the case may be. (ii) The use of the words " where the loss sustained is a loss of profits or gains" to be set aside against profits and gains would not be sufficient to restrict the scope of the main enactment, namely, section 24 which was to set off loss of profit or gains under any other head. It was then contended that in the proviso the words used were " where " the loss suffered is a losses of profits and gain ". The mere fact that the word " income " is not used does not justify the construction.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. The Head Office of the Company is at Calcutta. It has branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The general practice of the company both at the Head Office and the Branch Offices appears to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 though in certain cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees under which the age Of retirement was extended to 58 years subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the ageof 55. The first respondent raised a dispute regarding their retirement age but the Tribunal directed that the age should be 58 but the Company may in its wisdom and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was also found that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay region the trend had been to fix the retirement age at 60 years. The Tribunal further directed that in view of this finding of the Tribunal that in some of its earlier decisions as to the relevant trend in the Bombay region was accurate, the Tribunal took into account the fact that in the awards recent times there was a general agree ment that the date of retirement should be fixed at 60 and not at 55. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the decision of this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen ; , relied on by the Tribunal was erroneous as the facts and circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on record clearly showed a consistent trend in Bombay regions region to fix its retirement age. Held, further, that the Tribunal had taken considerable pains to perform this duty and it had ultimately persuaded itself to hold that no such trend was established in fact. Dunzoop Rubber Company Ltd., v The Workmen ; and Dunzyop Rubber CO. Ltd. vs Workmen, [1960] 2 S.C.R. 869, relied on.

The appellant company was appointed as the Managing Director of the Company from December 5, 1961 and his appointment and remuneration were approved by the Central Government on July 30, 1962. The Board of Directors of the company in pursuance of a collaboration agreement between it and the company entered into an agreement with M/s. L. A. Mitchell Ltd., for importing the requisite machinery was granted to the Company. On June 4, 1965, the company preferred a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the Punjab High Court for quashing the order dated May 19, 1965. The High Court rejected the contentions urged before it on behalf of the appellant and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave: Held: (i) The power conferred on the Central Govern ment by section 237(b) to order an investigation and delegated by it to the company Law Board is administrative, that it can be validly exercised by the Chairman of the Board by an order made in pursuance Of a rule enacted by the central Government under section 642(1) read with section 10E(5), that the exercise of the power does not violate any fundamental right of the respondent; (ii) The powers are exercised for ascertaining facts and, therefore before they are finally known all that is necessary for the exercise Of the powers is the opinion of the board that there are circumstances which suggest to it that fraud and other kinds of mismanagement mentioned in sub cls. If the facts do reasonably suggest any of these things to the Board, the power can be exercised, although another individual might think that the ;facts suggest otherwise it cannot be said that from a huge loss incurred by a company and the working of the companies in a disorganised and un businegslike way, the only conclusion possible is that it was due to lack of capability. The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to five years rigorous imprisonment. The High Court drew from this conclusion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits, and convicted them accordingly under section 396 of the Penal Code. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the presumption under section 41 1 722 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or at the most tinder section 412 of the I.P.C., but not of complicity in the crime of dacoity. HELD: The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence to connect an accused with the crime itself, however small, the finding of stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. [723 E] In the present case the goods stolen were a large quantity of cloth taken for sale to the market. These goods were not sold and were being taken back to the dealers by the cartmen.) A large number of persons said to be 20 in number pelted stones at the cart men and looted the property. It was impossible to think that within the short time available, these goods could have been easily disposed of to receivers of stolen properties or could be placed in the custody of friends till such time as the original offenders could take them away.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Section 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. Under the provisions thereof, the Collector must make his award within two years from the date of the publication of the declaration and that if no award is made within that period, the entire proceedings for acqui sition of the land shall lapse. The petitioners obtained an interim order from this Court directing status quo with regard to the possession of the lands in question in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1985 preferred against the said order of the Karnataka High Court dated August 14, 1984. On December 16, 1987, two writ petitions were filed by the respective petitioners in the Karnataka high Court challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards were not made within the stipulated time. The learned Single Judge dismissed the petitions on October 6, 1989 and November 29, 1988. In these two writ Petitions, the KarnatakaHigh Court granted interim stay of further proceedings in respect of the acquisition of the said lands. In the Special Leave Petitions preferred against this order of dismissal, the petitioners have filed these Special Leave petitions. Dismissing the Special leave petitions, the Court, ^ HELD: 1. The relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [566D] 2. In view of the provisions in Section 11 A of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, to which we have already referred earlier, it is beyond dispute that the fact of the stay orders was highly material in the determination of these Special leave Petitions. The respondents made applications under section 33 C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 praying for determination and computation of the benefit to which they were entitled under the Desai Award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal. The Desai award dealt with the method of fitment provided in cl. (iv) and made clause (4 A). The workmen 's basic pay as on January 1, 1959 was Rs. 106. He would not be entitled to any increments under sub cls. (a), (b) and (c) because his actual salary coincided with the adjusted basic pay in the Sastry award scale as modified on January l, 1959. Held, that the adjustment basic pay under cl. 5 of the Desai award must be read as on February 1, 1960. The adjusted basic Pay in cl.(ii) has to be taken as on December 1, 1950. This follows from the fact that the workman 's salary has to he fixed as on March 1,1959. In view of cl. 2(iv) his salary has necessarily to be fixed as On January 1. 1959. The adjustment under sub el. (b), has to take effect and give two annual increments for 1960 and 1961 which are beyond the date which we have interpreted in Prakash Chand Mehra 's case. Prakash Chand Mehta vs Prakash Chand Shah, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 986, State Bank of India vs Prakashchand Mehra, ; , State Bank Of India vs Parkash Chand Mehra, [1964] 1 S.L.J. 891 and State Bankof India vs Ram Prakash Chand, [1963] Supp, 3 S.T.R., referred to.

The assessee, Dr. R.S. Gupta had maintained an account in the books of Messrs. Tika Ram and Sons Pvt. Ltd., and there was no dispute that instructions of the assessee were car ried out by the Company and relevant debit entries and credit en tries were made in the respective accounts. On 1st January 1957, Om Prakash Gupta wrote to the assessee, his father, thanking him for the gift of Rs.25,000 made in his favour and the gift was effected by debiting the assessee 's personal account in his books and corresponding credits to the accounts of L and K. With effect from 28th March, 1957, the assessee had a substantial credit balance of Rs., 1,50,000 which he purported to give to his son. The Gift Tax Officer rejected the contention that the gift made by transfer entries in the ' books of account and by the declaration, did not operate to bring into existence a valid gift. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was valid gift but in that case it was a banking company. The High Court in reference affirmed the view taken by the Tribunal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In cases of entries in books of accounts by credit and debit, the sums should be available on the date of gift in the account of the firm whose accounts are said to be credited or debited. [127E] 2. Where the assessee has a credit amount with firm or with family or with a banking Company and that sum is available to that firm or the company or H.U.F. on the dates of the gift, then a valid Gift by book entries might be possible but where a sum was not available with the firm or family or a company which was not a banking firm or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entries even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid transfer. [128F] 2:1 In the instant case, the High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. The order and judgment of the High court are set aside. All the questions are answered in favour of the revenue.

Section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913 as it originally stood underwent substantial changes in 1960 and as a result thereof, a host of writ petitions 122 were filed in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the constitutional validity of section 15 on the ground that it infringed Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitu tion. The appellant contended that since the suit land belonged to more than one co sharer and had not been sold jointly by all the co sharers, he was entitled to claim the right of pre emption under clause 'fourthly ' of section fifteen(1) (b). A similar question came up before this Court in Balwant Ram vs B. Baijnath Singh, ; , wherein a two judge Bench negatived the contention that it cannot stand after the pronouncement of this Court on the expression 'other co sharors ' in section 15(i)(b) and is therefore entitled to exercise the right conferred on him by that provision. The question was whether the suit lands belonged to different persons or not. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The object of the Legislature was to confer the right to pre empt on specified family members of the vendor or vendors in the first three clauses of section15(1). Under the Punjab Act, 1905, the corresponding provision, section 12, con ferred a right of preemption, in the case of a sale of a share of such land or properly held jointly, firstly in the lineal discendents of the vendee in male line in order of succession; secondly, in persons not included under first or second above, in order to of succession and thirdly, in other co shar ers jointly or severally. It will be noticed that priority for the exercise of the right owes statutorily fixed and even in the cases of those falling within the same class, the exercise Of right was regulated by the use of the expression, 'in order of inheritance '. The 1905 Act was repealed and replaced by the 1913 Act. Accord ing to section 15 of this Act before its amendment in 1960, in case of sale of share out of joint land or property, the right was conferred firstly on the lineal descendents who held under tenancy of the vendors or vendors; secondly in the co divideders jointly and severally. [123D E] 1.2. The expression ' other co Tra sharers ' was used in the fourth clause of the said provision to ensure that no co shar er is left out or omitted and not to deny the right teen to kinstolk cosharers covered by the preceding clauses. If the preceding clause were not erased from the statute book as unconstitu tional the kinsfolk would have exercised the right in the order of preference, for which no justification was found. [124E F] 1:3.

The workmen of the appellant company, who was a manufacturer of glass industry, were not entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days. The Company 's claim for sickness leave was resisted by the companies on the ground that the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of the , were already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. The company also contended that section 99 of the Act gave wide powers to the Employees ' State Insurance Corpora tion to enhance the benefit and it was therefore the proper authority to examine the demand. The workmen of that Company had benefited a lot under the entire scheme of the . It was also urged that section 97 gave wide power to the employees ' State insurance Corpora tation to enhance tho benefit and, therefore, the company should not be said to have erred in restoring the benefit which the workmen were entitled under the award of 1958. The Tribunal rejected the contention of the Company that as the benefits were already available to the workmen in the Baroda with retrospective effect from Decem ber 14,1969, they were very much more adequate and the Tribunal was justified in granting additional benefits. On appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as section 99 gave wide discretion to the workers ' State ' Insurance Corporation to enhance their benefit and that the workmen did not deserve anything more than sickness benefit. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said tO cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the Tribunal. [83B] 2.1 In providing for periodical payments to an insured worker in case of sickness (sickness benefit) or for medical treatment or attendance to him or the members of his family, the legislature did not intend to substitute any of these benefits for the workmen 's right to get leave on full pay on the grounds of sickness. [86C] 2:2 The benefit of sick leave was therefore lost when the Act was made applicable to the region from December 1, 1969. That was obviously under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefits which the Act allowed for, as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the demand for sickness benefit and does not, at any rate, provide for grant of leave on Full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness.

The appellant was detained under the order of detention passed by the Government of Bombay on the 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were vague and there was no application of mind by the detaining authority to the existence or otherwise of the legitimate objects of detention. Held, that the obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest, are vested in the detaining Authority not in any other. It was therefore necessary for the detaining authorities to have an idea of the grounds of preventive detention as furnished. The requirement for such a communication would arise only if the detenue feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. An obligation to communicate the decision not to disclose facts considered prejudicial to public interest may well be implied in such a situation. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue, the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right of representation and an obligation to supply particulars has been recognised in the case of the State of Bombay vs Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya (A.I.R. , referred to. Held further that the requirement for making a representation under article 22(5) of the Constitution on behalf of the Portuguese Government by means of his affidavit filed in the High Court was without any basis, in view of the affidavit of the Chief Secretary. The order of the detention was mala fide and was passed for the ulterior purpose of preventing the appellant from acting in any manner prejudicial to the security of India and to the relations of India with Portugal.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows : "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer, Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He then took her in his scooter to the unit lines of 51 1 Gurkha Rifles where he arranged her meeting with a tea shop nearby where she received a present of sari and blouse from the sepoys in his presence. " The respondent was charged under section 120B, I.P.C., for having committed acts which were gross misconduct and as such dismissed from service. The Central Government found it to be unsatisfactory and on April 9, 1959 an order was passed removing the respondent from service by the appellant. The respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for quashing the order of removal from service on the ground that r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954, was ultra vires the . The High Court allowed the petition holding that r, 14 of Army Rules was ultra rites and that the action taken thereunder was without any authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45 and the Central Government had thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. HELD : The power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words 'subject to . , it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. For removal from the serv ice under section19 of the read with r.14 of the . Rules, the Central government may remove a "person from the Service". Rule 14 is such a rule : it is not ultra vires. It is not correct to say that there should be rules and subject to the provision of the Act and such rules, the C. Government may dismiss or remove from the services any person subject to this Act.

The appellant was a Panchayat under the C.P. & Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. On June 1, 1959, the Bombay Village Panchayat Act 1958 (Bombay Act III of 1959) came into effect in Vidharba region and by virtue of this Act the appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat. On July 14, 1961, the Panchayat passed resolution No. 2 with a view to levy octroi duty. The resolution further stated that the appellant 's appeal to the Standing Committee was rejected on September 4, 1963. Thereafter, the appellant filed an appeal before the Standing committee under section 124(5) of the Act before the Panchayat Samiti, Parseoni. The Standing Committee allowed the appeal of the Company on two grounds: (1) that it was necessary for the Panchayat to have the octroi limits fixed with the approval of the Collector before levying octroi under r. 21; and (2) that the approval was given by the Collector on January 14, 1964 relating back to April 1, 1963, and therefore the levy of octroi from April 1. 1963 was regularised. The appellant contended that r. 5 of the Fees Rules was ultra vires the powers of the rule making authority. Held:(i) The Standing committee inspected the premises of the company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity. (ii) Rule 5 of Rules framed under section 176(2)(XV) of C. P.C., does not require the Panchayat concerned to fix the octroi limit in the resolution passed under r .3(a). It only deals with two items, namely, (1 ) selection of the tax and the rate at which it is to be levied; and the rates at which the tax or fee to be imposed and the amount at which a tax is to levied. The inhabitants of the village would be entitled to object only to these two matters, namely (a) the tax, or fee imposed and (b) the rate. But the learned counsel for the appellant contended (i) that r . 5 was ultra rites as it had failed to fix octroi limits in accordance with law; (ii). that the Standing Committees were entitled to deal with the appeal on merits; (iii) that there was no proper publication under r, 4 of the Rules was announced by beat of drum in the village and (iv) that in any event the Collector could regularise an imposition made without the authority of law.

The appellant was dismissed by the Conciliation Officer under section 33(1) read with section 33 (1) of the , and on appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment of acquittal. Held, that the conciliation proceedings were pending at the time when the report under section 12(6) was made by the conciliation officer but when that report was received by the appropriate Government, it was not open to the Government to terminate the conciliation proceeding after 14 days but only terminated as provided in section 20(2)(b) of tile Act. Workers of the Industry Dhanbad vs Management of the Colliery, ; , referred to. The conciliation proceedings therefore did not end when the conciliation report under s.12(6), was made and when that Report was received, by the Government, the dismissal could not be said to be one within the words " pendency of any conciliation proceedings ". The Act provided for commencement and conclusion of conciliation proceedings under section 20 but the first sub section of section 20 deals with what are called utility services and sub section 2 of that provides as to when the Conciliation proceedings conclude. That sub section is as follows: section 20 (1). . . . , . . A conciliation proceeding shall be deemed to have concluded in the case where no settlement is reached, when a memorandum of the settlement is signed by the par ties to the dispute; and (b) where no settle ment is arrived at, when the Report under section12( 6) is made by an Conciliation Officer but when the reference is made to a Court Labour Court, Tribunal or National Tribunal under section 10 during the pendency of conciliation proceeding.

On 24.12.1985, between 10 and 10.30 A.M., the subject alongwith Ramashish Bangali, Gulam Rambriksha armed with Rifle, gun etc. came in car No. BHG 9372 on Katras Coal Dump and started indiscriminate firing to kill Birendra Pratap Singh a rival of his calendestine business of coal to establish his criminal superiority in full view of the shopkeepers, customers and passers by of the area. The petitioner/appellant made representation on 22nd January, 1986 and the appellant was informed that the said representation was rejected. Thereafter, the petitioner 's matter was referred to the Advisory Board. The order of detention was passed on an incident relating to exchange of fire between two rival groups. A criminal case had been registered in relation to the said incident pursuant to which the petitioner was already in custody. The detention order though dated 2nd January 1986 was served on or about 11th January,1986, it was served only on or after 11th February, 1986. It is the case of the petitioner that the detenu was not served with all the documents referred to and/or relied on. The detenu was served with the order of approval of the said order of his detention by the Government of Bihar. The appellant/petitioner contended that the order could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1(a) The power of directing preventive detention given to the appropriate authorities must be exercised in exceptional cases as contemplated by the various provisions of the different statutes dealing with preventive detention and should be used with great deal of circumspection. There must be awareness of the facts necessitating preventive custody of a person for social defence. If a man is in custody and there is no imminent possibility of his being released, the power of preventive detention should not be exercised. [908C D] (b) The order dated 2.1.1986 was served upon the detenu on or before 11th of January, 1987. It does not appear that either the prospect of immediate release of the detenu or other factors which can justify the detention of a man in detention were properly considered in the light of the principles noted in the aforesaid decision and especially in Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District Magis trate Etah & Ors., W.P. (Crl.) No. 2 96/86 dt 25.9.86 and Raj Kumar Singh vs The State of Bihar & Ors. Crl A. 353/86 with W. P. (crl) 27/86 dated 26th September, 1986, referred to. (c) In the instant case, when the actual order of deten tion was served against the detenu, the detenu had already surrendered in respect of the criminal charge against him. At the relevant time, the appellant/ petitioner was undertrial in the said criminal case. There is no indication that this factor or the question that the impugned detenu might be released or that there was such a possibility of release, was taken into consideration by the detaining Authority properly and seriously before the service of the order. [09D E] (d) The grounds for forming the satisfaction for the need for the detention were there, and there was rational nexus between the object of the Order as contemplated under the Act and the materials on record. Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The section does not provide nor is any rule brought to our notice which enjoins upon the Administrator to give a hearing to dealer who seeks permission under this Section and give reasons in case he decides to refuse the permission. [955E] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asstt. Collector of Central Excise, Poona II Division while declaring unamended section 27(6) of the Act invalid on the ground that it suffers from the vice of excessive delegation of legislative power inasmuch as no criteria or guide lines have been provided by reference to which the power conferred upon the administrator to refuse permission or grant permission should be exercised and that the section confers an unguided, uncanalised, uncanalalised power upon the authority with the result that the licensed dealer is at his mercy while seeking permission to carry on money lending or banking business on the security of any article, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as such dealer. The High Court struck down section 28 in the manner done and in its judgment the High Court. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the impugned section is violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as it suffersfrom the vice vice of delegation of power inasmuch that no criteria have been laid down by reference. It was further submitted that even though import of gold into India had been banned considerable quantities of contraband gold were found finding their way into the country through illegal channels affecting the national economy and hampering the country 's economic stability and progress, that the Customs Department was not in a position to effectively combat the smuggling over the long borders and coast line, that therefore anti smuggling measures had to be supplemented by a detailed system of control over internal transactions and that therefore Anti smuggling measures have to be replaced by a elaborate system of Control over internal dealings and that in the absence of parity of situation or circumstances the doctrine of parity cannot be invoked. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The objective underlying the policy and the scheme of the statute together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention of the other provisions of the , afford more than sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. [961D] Harkchand Ratan Chand Banthria vs Union of lndia, ; and Ramanlal Purshottamamdas Chokshi vs Union ondia & Ors., ; , referred to. 1.2 The policy and scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the Scheme affords sufficient guidance in the matters of exercising the discretion conferred on him under section. The main object in putting the Act on Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of the production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. " In the instant case, section 28 cannot be struck down on the grounds of excessive delegated delegation of any legislative power and its validity has to be upheld.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple, filed a suit against four respondents for possession of certain properties in the Court of the District Munsif at Turaiyur. The trial court held that the grant of the Inam was a personal inam and that it was not a grant in favour of the religious endowment within the meaning of the Act. On appeal by the appellants to the High Court, the lower appellate court reversed the finding of the lower Appellate Court that the existence of the temple had not been proved. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The properties belonged to the temple; that they have been transferred for valuable consideration. [123 B] (ii) Article 134 B applied to all cases where it is shown that the immovable property was comprised in the endowment and that the transfer was effected by a previous manager; and that, therefore, limitation began as soon as the purchaser took possession of the office adversely to the plaintiff. [124 C D] Gnanasambanda Pandara Sannadhi vs Velu Pandanam & Another, ; , referred to. (iii) The question whether article 134 B applies to a case where debuttar property had been sold in an execution sale and the Privy Council held that it did not. [125 E F] Ganasamandaswamiar had resigned his position about 27 years ago, and that even if article 134B applied, limitation should be held to have commenced from the date when the alienor either resigned his office or was removed from it. In the present case, what had been transferred by the manager on the basis that it belonged to him and not to the religious endowments, but on the evidence led in relation to this aspect of the matter, the learned trial Judge has examined the oral evidence led on behalf of the parties. He assumed that Pachaikandaswami or his son were alive at the date of the suit. Even so, he found that they had left the village and had taken no part whatever in the management of the worship of the Temple. [126 G H] (iv) The contention that article 134 A did not apply to a present case because the alienations evidenced by Exts. A 3, A 6 and A 12 show that the alienors purported to transfer the properties not as Poojaris or managers of a Temple but in their individual character as owners of the said properties. [127 G H; 128 A] (v) The High Court was in error in reversing the decisions of the courts below by holding that the title of the deity had not be lost by adverse possession before the suit was filed.

The appellants were displaced persons and on 30 8 1952 the respondent issued a notice to the appellants calling upon them to show cause why the lease should not be cancelled and why they should not he evicted. The notice then went on to state that the respondent considered it necessary to issue certain directions for the "preservation of the demised premises and the goods and stock in trade etc., lying in the demised Premises, and called upon them, to showcause why the leases should not been cancelled and that they should be evicted. On 13 2 1954 the appellants appeared before the respondent and contended that he had no auth ority to issue the notice in question under section 12 of the , and that it was therefore illegal. Apprehending that the lease might be cancelled, the appellants filed an application for a writ of certiorari for quashing the notice dated 13 21954 issued by the Custodian. The High Court held that on the plain language of section 12 it would apply whenever there was a lease, and that lease was in respect of property belonging to the evacuee, that there was no warrant for imposing a further limitation on that section that lease should also have been granted by the evacuee and not by the respondent himself, and therefore the Custodian had power under section 10 to cancel the agreement to sell the mills and the factory to them. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the Custodian has the power and had always the power to cancel leases created not merely by the evacuees but also by himself. But he is acting within his authority in issuing Exhibit C in so far as it concerned the lease granted in favour of the appellants was valid. Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs Arabinda Bose, ; , referred to.

The appellant, a minor son of Raghubir Singh, was born to Raghubir Singh on 14th March, 1963 and was only 13 years of age when the ceiling proceedings were finalised by the Sub Divisional Officer on 5th May, 1976. He further held that the provisions of the old ceiling law applied to the case but the Sub division Officer had committed an error of law in determining the ceiling area under the new law i.e. the Act of 1955. The Board went on to hold that there was no provision for separate units in Chapter III B of the Act, of 1955 and the applicant Raghubir Singh and his son Surendrapal Singh constituted one unit and not two units and the case was remanded to Sub Divisional officer, Hanumangarh, for fresh determination of the calling area for Raghubir Singh. Before the Division Bench of the High Court in the writ petitions it was urged on behalf of Raghubir singh that the power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board could not be exercised to the detriment of the writ petitioners much less by way of suo motu exercise of powers. The High Court held that there is no provision in Chapter II B of Rajasthan Tenancy Act, 1955 and that the Board of Revenue had appellate jurisdiction and it could not, therefore, make use of its powers of superintendence and Control and the order of the Board. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1. Section 221 of the Rajasthan Tenancy Rules, 1955 is similar to section 107 of the Government of India Act, 1915 in the Act. [728G] 2. The power is there, and it may be exercised sparingly in extraordinary case where interest of justice requires that the board should exercise the power. Under section 107, the Government has general powers of supervision and control of all revenue Courts. It is both administrative as well judicial powers. It was open to the Board to exercise its powers on all its subordinate courts in order to regulate the functioning of subordinate courts so as to keep them within their respective spheres of jurisdiction. If the subordinate court disregards any specific provision of law and does something illegal it is open to it to the board of Revenue to interfere and set the matter right. [628G H] 3. The appeal consequently fails and is dismissed with costs.

The expression "newspaper" is defined by section 2(b) of the Act as any working journalist, and includes any other person employed to do any work in, or in relation to, any newspaper establishment. "Newspaper establishment" is a newspaper establishment under the control of any person or body of persons whether incorporated or not, for the production or publication of one or more newspapers or for conducting any news agency or syndicate. The expression "working journalist" is not defined in the Act. Several definitions of the expression "New 'spaper ' and "new 's newspaper establishment" are given before this Court. In order to be a newspaper, a work must be a " printed work". (i) a periodical; and (ii) should contain public news or comments on public news. Any other class of printed periodical work as may, from time to time, be notified in this behalf by the Central Government in the Official Gazette. The definition of the word "new" is also not defined. In the instant case, the law reports published by the Ist respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first respondent in their production or publishing of the said law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the central Government on the basis of the recommendations made by the Palekar Award. The first respondent submitted its reply in October 1981 inter alia contending that it was not running a newspaper Establishment and publications published by it were not the newspapers and as such the Perelekar Award was not applicable to it. Again on 18th November, 1982 the Deputy Labour Commissioner wrote to the 1st respondent asking it to file its written statements in the matter of non implementation of the Peealekar award as the orders of the Central government made under section 12 of the . The first Respondent submitted its written statement in October, 1981 inter mainly contending that the law Reports publised by it contained information about the recent events which had taken place in the Supreme Court or in the High Courts which were public bodies and those matters in which the public was interested. The 1st Respondent also did not send a reply to the questionnaire issued by the Tribunal nor gave any evidence before the Tribunal in respect of the matters referred to therein. However on 15th July, 1981 the Deputy Commissioner wrote a letter to the Manager of the 1 st respondent informing him that the 1St respondent was liable to implement the order of the central government made on the recommendations of the palekar Tribunal in regard of its employees since the Ist Respondent was a newspaper industry establishment. Immediately after the service of the notice, the Ist respon dent filed a writ petition before the High Court questioning the validity of the notices served on it by the Deputy labour Commissioner calling upon it to implement its orders of Central Government on its basis of recommendations of Justice Paleyan Tribunal. The High Court accepted the plea of the Istst Respondent and declared that the Law reports were not newspapers within the meaning of section 2 (b)of the Act and that the demand made by it was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. Aggrieved by the decision of the High court the appellants have filed this appeal by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports are published by publication in the law books which they come to know of the latest legal position prevailing in the country on any question decided in the decisions reported in the said reports. Hence it is difficult to agree with the submission made on behalf of the first Respondent that since the law report are going to be preserved by the lawyers as reference books after getting them rebound subsequently they should be treated as books. It may be that the decisions contained in these law reports may cease to be items of news after some time but when they are received by the subscribers they do possess the character of works containing news.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th of February, 1966 a fresh document of that date was executed and it was alleged that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years and whereas the licensor had agreed to allow him to occupy and use the said property for the period of 5 years. Clause 2 of the agreement recited that the licensee had agreed, to use the premises as above and merely for the purposes of workshop business. It further goes on to state that the "licensee shall not under any circumstances be allowed to use, the premises for residential purposes or any other purpose save and except specified therein". The period of leave and licence was to commence from 1st September, 1965 to 31st August, 1970 and it Was further submitted that the appellant had agreed that he would pay to the licensor a monthly compensation of Rs.225 per month. The licensor had also agreed to permit the licensee, who had approached the licensor to allow the licensee for use and occupation the said demised premises for a term of five year from 1 st September, 1966 till 31st of August, 1971, that agreement was being executed. It is alleged that this agreement was entered into between the parties since the respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits. The appellant had been described as the licensee ' and the recitals therein recite that the lessor was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant. The respondent filed an ejectment proceeding against the appellant under section 41 of the . It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent was not the owner of the workshop and also denied that he had given the workshop to him for conducting business. The submission was that there was sub tenancy by the respondent in favour of the appel lant as a monthly licensee of the business with articles and machinery belonging to the appellant and not to the respondent. On those grounds it was contended that ejectment proceedings were liable to be rejected. It Was further contended that the tenant was entitled to protection under the Rent Act but only the subtenancy as such and therefore it was recorded that as agreed 'B.C. no preliminary issue was framed to be framed. The trial Judge held that the agreement was a licence and not a licence. The High Court also rejected the contention of the respondent that he was a tenant and having found that the period was of licence had come to an end, he passed an order of eviction against the appe lant. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 It is well settled that in determining whether an agreement creates between the par ties the relationship of landlord and tenant or merely that of licensor and licensee the decisive consideration is the intention of the parties. [1062E] 1.2 In order to go back to the findings of the trial court, the Court of Small Causes and the High Court should not exercise jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution over such decision. [ 1063F] 1:3 The intention of parties was the real test for ascertaining the character of a document. It has been well settled in Halsbury 's Laws of England, Fourth Edition, Volume 27 page 13.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of Dholpur. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former Virpur State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. It was also the practice in that State that when permits for export were issued, export duties had to be paid in advance though the actual export was made later. The respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni before December 2, 1947. Thereafter he could not export further as his permit was not extended. He was also not able to export the entire quantity of 15.000 maund 's for which the permit was granted; he could only export 4,572 maunds and 20 seers of chiuni before the 30th December, 1947, but could only exported 4,574 maunds after December 2. The State did not pay back the amount due to the respondent. In the meantime, the United State of Rajasthan became the Part B State of Raj on January 26, 1950 when the Constitution came into force. The United State was formed by Covenant entered into by 14 Rulers of Rajasthan including these who had formed the Former State of India and which came into existence from April 7, 1949. It may be mentioned here that when this State came into operation on April 7. 1949 it provided for the continuance of all laws till they were repealed or amended by the new State. The Ruler of Dhol purpur State continued all the old laws till them were altered or modified, and there was specific provision in each Covenant that the assets and liabilities of the covenanting States shall be the assets of the new state of Matsya. Thereafter the United States of Rajasthan merged into the United Provinces of Rajasthan through the Matsya Union. The former Dhol purged the rights of the subjects of the old State flowing from the old law and was prepared to undertake the liability that may lie on it in consequence thereof. The new State continued the existing laws subject to their being altered or repealed by the old state. It also became a separate entity till March 17, 1948, though it had acceded to the Dominion of India after August 15, 1947 with respect to three subjects namely communications, defence and external affairs. In 1949, however, the process of merger in Rajasthan began and the first merger that took place was of the latter States of Alwar Bharatpur, Dholpur and Karauli which formed the Matsyas Union as from March 18, 1948 by a Covenant entered on February 28, 1948. The appellant applied for refund of Rs. 20,855/ along with interest and costs. The suits were resisted by the State on various grounds; but the High Court allowed the appeals holding that the agreement was not a law. It further held that there was no recognition by the respondent of the concessions by the newly formed sovereign and was not bound by any obligation against the old sovereign of the erstwhile State unless it chose to recognise the obligation. The present appeal was filed on special leave granted by this Court. Held, that the new sovereign throughout this process of integration from 1948 to 1950 must be taken to have recognised the rights Of the subjects and undertaken the liability, if any, of the existing States. M/s Dalmia Dadri Cement Co. Ltd. vs The Commissioner of Incometax, [1959] S.C.R. 729, followed. Held further that the old Indian laws were always to continue till they are repealed or altered by the fresh State. If the intention was otherwise, it should have found a provision similar to that in the Covenant in question by which all the new States were merged except Patiala and the Patila laws were to continue until they were altered, repealed or modified. The fact that the previous laws were continued till they became repealed or changed, did not alter the constitutional limitations. M.

The appellants, who were running a market as an occupation or business with high standards and that the notification directing the constitution of a Market Committee at Virudhunagar was challenged by them in the High Court. The High Court dismissed their applications. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the restrictions imposed by section 5 are not only unreasonable but tend to defeat the very purpose of the legislation; and (ii) the impugned provisions of section 5 were not only reasonable but tend also to defeat its object. Held:(i) The contentions raised in the appeals must be negatived. (ii)(a) The contention that the appellants had really two fundamental rights was not correct as they were not prohibited from holding the market as property, for they could still do business in the market subject to the regulations and also do business outside the prescribed area ; and (b) the provisions of the Act constitute reasonable restrictions on a citizen 's right to do business. The impugned provisions fall under two groups: the first group provides the machinery for controlling the trade in commercial crops and the second group of provisions imposes restrictions on the carrying on of the said trade. Section 14 says "No person shall, within a notified area, set up, establish or use, or continue or allow to be continued, any place for the purchase or sale of a notified commercial crop except under and in accordance with the conditions of a licence granted to him by the Collector. The second proviso enables the Market Committee to exempt from the provisions Of the above sub section any person who carries on the business of purchasing or selling any commercial crop in quantities not exceeding those prescribed by Rules made under the Act. The third proviso authorises the said Committee to remove from the purview of the sub section a person who is having a licence to trade,in and about the place where the market is fixed, is deprived of his livelihood which is an unreasonable restriction upon his right to doing business. But in the present case the appellants were not prevented from carrying on their business as they could not be said to have carried on their trade. The Act was an integrated one and it regulates the buying and selling of commercial crops. If the small traders are exempted, it creates loopholes in the scheme through which the big trader may operate, and thereby the object itself would be defeated. That apart, the second proviso enabled the Committee to exclude small traders in appropriate cases.

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death under section 302 of the Indian Penal Code. The High Court confirmed their conviction on the ground that they had been rightly convicted. Held, that in a case like that one there must be direct proof of prior concert or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference, or as we prefer to put it in the time honoured way, "the incriminating facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis". The evidence showed that the injury caused death was the one on the neck. All the eye witnesses were agreed that there was a large crowd there. There was no evidence of any prior meeting. It could not therefore be said that the simple rustics should get confused and not remember in minute detail exactly what they had stated from stage to stage. But the major part of their story hangs together remarkably well despite the many attempts to trip them in cross examination in the various courts. As a matter of fact, there was no special rule of evidence for this class of case. In the present case, the facts disclosed did not warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. The injuries on the throat having been accounted for, it could be relied on. The evidence of Rasika and Subhana were telling the truth and that they could be relying on. There is no reason to depart from this practice in this case and so reduce the sentences of death in the case of Bhilia and Tukia to transportation for life because of the difference of opinion in the High Court, not only on the question of guilt but also on that of sentence. In saying this we do not intend to fetter the discretion of judges in this matter, for a question of sentence is, and must always remain, a matter Of discretion unless the law directs otherwise. But when appellate Judges who agree on the questions of guilt differ on that question of death, it is usual not to impose the death penalty unless there are compelling reasons.

The petitioner was an Engineer who was employed in the Central Public Works Department under the Ministry of Works and Housing in Government of India. He was compulsorily retired by order dated 3.8.1976 with effect from 5.11.76 made under Rule 56(j) of the Fundamental Rules. The petitioner challenged that order for retirement and has claimed payment of remuneration which he would have been entitled to draw upto the normal date of superannuation. The vires of Rule 56 (j) as also the power to compulsorily retire a public servant have been upheld by this Court in several cases. In the instant case, the petitioner was promoted as officiating Assistant Engineer on 25.5.1954 and came to be confirmed as Section Officer by an order dated 8.10.1955. The validity of Rule 55(j)(i) has no application to officiating Government servants, hence can have no appli cation to the petitioner since the petitioner is an officiating government servant. " The appropriate authority is entitled to exercise power under clause (j). in the case of a Government servant in Class I or Class II service or post where he entered into service before attaining the age of 35 years after the said servant attained the age Of 50 years, and in other cases after he has attained the said age of fifty years. In these writ petitions, the petitioners would have retired from service and, therefore, they cannot be resorted in service. They would, however, be entitled to pecuniary benefit of salary and allowances admissible under the rules. Accordingly, the Writ Petitions are dismissed.
