The respondent filed a suit for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India Ltd. and the first defendant in the suit from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s V.O Tractors Export, Moscow, the second defendant. The trial court decided the issue against the appellant and the order was confirmed in appeal by the High Court. In appeals to this Court it was contended that an order granting interim injunction "is final" as far as this Court is concerned determining the rights of parties within the meaning of article 133(1)(a) and (b). HELD: The expression "final order" in article 133 (1) (a) means a final adjudication by the court of the rights, of the parties in dispute in a suit or proceeding; if the rights and obligations of the party in dispute have to be determined, the order is interlocutory. [703 B] Mohanlal Maganlal Thakkar vs State of Gujarat, ; , applied. In the instant case not even an issue has been decided and it was not contended that the order of the High court amounts to a judgment or "a decree". The order refusing to grant an interim ' injunction did not determine the rights & obligations of parties in relation to the matter in dispute. [ 703 C D] Mohanlal Shamlal Thakkar & Ors. vs State o Gujarat, [1958] S.C.R. 1007 and Druva Coal Company vs Benaras Bank, ; referred to.

In respect of the civil miscellaneous petition for clarification of this Court 's judgment dated 4th November, 1988, it was made clear that the assessable value of the processed fabric would be the value of grey cloth plus the value in the hands of the processor plus the price of the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses. That would be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessablevalue of the processing fabric and excise duty would be charged to the processor on that basis provided that the declaration as to the price at which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, would include only the price or deemed price at that which the processed fabrics would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the prices at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabil ities under the said Act and the rules made thereunder. The price at Which he is selling his goods must be the price for of the grey cloth or fabric plus the values of the raw job work worked plus manifufac tion expenses. Rule 173 of the Rules enjoins that if the value value of a grey cloth in the hand of the operator is Rs.20 and the value is the value, of the dye work done is Rs .5 and the manufacturing profit and expenditure expenses for the processing be Rs.5, then in such a case the value would be Rs .30, being the value as of the finished product plus the cost of the machine worked plus the manufacturing profits and the manufacture expenses but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It was also necessary to include the processor "s profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits. The Department gate here here here means means the "deemed" factory gate as if the processed textile fabric is sold by the processor.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending Act deleted section 33 of the Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayats. The appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed on April 1, 1975, and therefore entitled to be absorbed in Government service as a Clerk in any event. But, as a result of the deletion of section 33 by the Amending Acts of 1973, the Panchayat Raj Samiti lost its power to appoint him to the post. The fact that the appellant was promotion as a head clerk on an ex hoc basis cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending came into force. There is no substance in this contention. Even assuming for the purposes of argument that the right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to he considered for promotions but, whether the Panchayat had the right on June 13. 1973. [737E G] The fact of the appellant being promoted as Head Clerk prior to his absorption in Government Service has to be recognised and protected, despite the fact that such appointment was made after the Amending act came into effect.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity Sri Thakur Gokarneshwar Mahadeo Ji installed in the Math. The suit was contested by the first defendant, Kedar Nath Chaubey, also referred to as Uma Shankar Yati. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. It held that the Amauli properties had been purchased by Mahant Shivshankar Yati for Rs. 40,000 forming part of a fund left behind by his predecessor Sri Mahant Shivpher Yati and that the income from the properties belonging to the math and deity left any appreciable surplus after meeting the expenditure on account of bhog, arpan deepdan daily and annual puja and other obligations specified in the waqf deed. The present appeal is directed against that part of the judgment and order of the High Court. It was contended for the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nucleum and must, therefore, be regarded as property belonging to Math or the temple. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaiuli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Shiv Shankar Yatati who in 1921 employed it for the purchase of the Amaul properties. Mahant Shiv Shanker Yati executed a will in 1956 and it appears beyond dispute that by virtue of this will the Amahi properties devolved on Uma ShankarYati. It is pointed out before us that in assessment proceedings under the U. P. Agriculture Income Tax Act 1948, the Amaoli properties were described by Mahant Sheo Shankar Yutti as properties of the Math and therefore a claim to exemption from the levy was made. The question whether the fund was the personal Property of Mahant or deity is the personal properties of Mahant, the burden of proof resting on the party who makes the claim. [663D E] 2. In assessment proceedings tinder the U P. Agricultural Income Tax, Act 1948 the Amaiii properties were mentioned by Mahant Sri Shiv ShankarYathas Yati as properties and of the math or deity. The income from these properties was not challenged by the plaintiffs in the present suit.

The appellants were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 5 1/4 units in the village of Raikot in Ludhiana District in 1949. Their father Sardar Nand Singh who was 42 330 found entitled to quasi permanent allotments of 40 standard acres, and 5/4 unit of land was given quasipermanent allotment in another village named Humbran in the same district. The two villages were however, 25 miles or so distant from each other. Nand Singh made an application for consolidation of his lands with those of the appellants in the villages Raikot. During the pendency of this application he died and after his death, the application was continued by the appellants. This application was rejected by the Assistant Custodian on August 20, 1952. On December 17, 1954, the appellants applied to the Deputy Custodian General for a review of the order cancelling their allotment on the ground that the cancellation was a result of misapprehension of the actual facts and that they were not entitled to allotment of suburban land at all. The Additional Custodian rejected this application on the view that r. 14(6) of the Evacuee Property Rules which came into force on July 22, 1952 stood in the way of cancellation of the allotment in favour of the appellant. On January 6, 1955, the Deputy Commissioner cancelled the allotment of Raikkot lands made in favour Of the appellants automatically stood cancelled. The appellants then moved the Deputy Inspector General for calling up their review application and for revising the order of October 31, 1952 passed by the Additional Custodian cancelling the allotment. The revision application filed by the appellant was dismissed on August 21, 1952 on the grounds that r 14(1) of Evacuee Property Act which came in force on September 7, 1952, stood in it way of a cancellation of allotment in their favour by the order dated October 31. 1952. Held, that the powers conferred by section 19 of the 1954 Act are confined only to properties which are entrusted to them for management and not with respect to any other property. The power of the Custodian under the , to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment existing in favour is not conflict with section 10 of the in so far as the question of cancellation is concerned. Bal Mukund vs The State of Punjab, ; , referred to.

The petitioners were employees of the State Government. The Government had issued a notification dated October 29, 1979 stating that it had decided to reduce the age of superannuation of all Government employees, other than in the last grade Service from 58 to 58 years. Two notifications issued in exercise of the power conferred by the Proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution were appended to that order. The petitioners challenged the said orders and notifications on the ground that they violated Articles 14, 16, 21 and 300A of the constitution. The case of the petitioners was that there was no basis at all for reducing the age Of retirement from 58 and that the Government had exercised its power arbitrarily without having regard to factors which were relevant on the fixation of the age. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contention that the provisions of the Ordinance whereby the age was reduced from 55 to 55 years amounted to removal within the meaning of Article 311(2) is not hit by Article 14 or Article 16 since it is not arbitrary or unreasonable in the circumstances of the case. It is well settled that Article 311 (2) of the is attracted only when a civil servant is reduced in rank, dismissed or removed from service by way of penalty, that is to say, when the effect of the order passed against him in this behalf is to visit him with evil consequences. Besides, the point made by Shri Venugopal is concluded by a Constitution Bench decision of this Court in Bishun Narain Misra vs State of Uttar Pradesh [1971] 2 S.C.R. 869. The State Government had the relevant facts as also the reports of the various Central and State Pay Commissions before it, on the basis of which it had to take a reasonable decision. The contentions of the petitioner must lead to the conclusion that there has to be a uniform age of retirement all over India. If reduction of the retirement age from 58 years to 55 is to be regarded as arbitrary on the grounds that it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement age at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. [602C E] 1.2 The argument that the provision of the ordinance which was introduced into the Fundamental Rules was without any basis. It was not arbitrary and unreasonable in nature. The amendment made by the Government of Andhra Pradesh in exercise Of its powers conferred by it under the proviso to Article 311 read with article 313 of Constitution is beyond the powers of the rule making authority or the Legislature. [502D E] 2.1 In the instant case, the State Govern ment had the necessary facts as well as the reports submitted by the various States and State pay Commissions before the Court, on its basis of the which it has to take into consideration a reasonable view.

The appellants were registered dealers under the Indian Partnership Act. The Sales Tax Officer assessed them to sales tax on a taxable turnover including these sales. He also assessed them as being in excess of the prescribed period by anybody. The High Court dismissed their applications for writs for quashing the order of assessment and the notice of demand and for prohibiting the Sales Tax officer from taking any steps pursuant to the order or the notice. Held, that the words " a person " in section 8(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act as a " registered dealer" and that the purchasing dealers have rightly been assessed to purchase tax under section 10(b). The scheme of the Legislature clearly is that where the intention as declared has not been carried out purchase tax should be levied. To hold otherwise would be to make the declaration of the intention useless. [928 C] In the instant case the goods remained the sellers ' property till the goods had been brought and loaded on board the ship and so the sales were exempted from tax under article 286(1)(b) Of the Constitution. The normal rule in FOB contracts is that it is the duty of the buyer to obtain the necessary export licence. That was laid down in Brandt 's case (1) and though in a later case in Hardy vs Pound, , the Court of Appeal in England held that the judgment in BrandT 's Case did not cover every FOB contract and that in the special facts of the particular case before them it was for the sellers to obtain licence and this view was approved by the House of Lords.

The respondent husband married the appellant as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later had a son by her. The initial warmth vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted, marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat, a house in Bombay, to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a reference to mehar money (Rs. 5,000/ and 'iddat ' money) which was also stated to have been adjusted by the compromise terms. There were a clause in the compromise that the appellant declares that she has now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the respondent was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her mother for their subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay where the parties lived, was high, and that the Respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appel lant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband who on a strange view of the law that the court under section 125 had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The High Court rejected the revision petition and summarily dismissed a revision petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code which provides that "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by her husband and that she had received, whether before or after the date of the said order, the whole of the sum which under any customary or personal law applicable to the parties, was payable on such divorce cancel such order, (i) in the case where such sum was paid before such order from the date on which such order was made. (ii) in any other case from the dates of expiry of the period, if any, for which maintenance has been actually paid by the husband to the woman; and (iii) in a case from a date of expiry, if no maintenance had been actually payable by the wife to the women. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. In the normal course an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the Magistrate at the trial level. However, the husband has not examined himself to prove that he had been giving allowances to the divorced wife. His case, on the contrary, is that she bad forfeited her claim because of divorce and the consent decree. Obviously, he has no case of non neglect. His plea is his right to ignore.

The petitioner was given an opportunity to file his objections to the preliminary list. The High Court of Mysore held that the writ petition was premature as the final list of officers on an integrated seniority list was still to be prepared after hearing objections. The petitioner, who had retired from service, filed a Writ Petition in this Court challenging the validity of the final gradation list. It was contended by him that he was not heard after the final seniority list had been prepared and that the rules had not been complied with. Dismissing the writ Petition, HELD: 1.1 The combined final gradation List dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [829H; 830A] 1.2 In order to establish the invalidity of the provisional list on some such grounds of invalidity, those grounds have to be shown to exist. The Court cannot go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government. It would, therefore, be quite fair to give a person affected an 'oppo opportunity to be heard against the proposed final gradation before it is finalised so that any possible mistakes, either on facts relating to his particular case or of law in applying the rules governing seniority to those facts, may be rectified. But once he has had that opportunity, it cannot possibly be said that he should have a further opportunity against even a final seniority List. If he was to have that opportunity the list would not really be final but only provisional or preliminary. It will be obviously contradictory to hold it to be a final list and yet declare it subject to modifica tions on further objections. [ 830E F] 1:3 The combined tentative gradation list dated April, 1962 so faras category 6 in respect of category 6 was concerned, was ultra vires as well as illegal and illegal.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of gold. The Import & Export Policy for the period April, 1988 to March, 1991 was in para 174 made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said policy. One of the conditions for eligibility for grant or entitlement of an export house certificate was that the import of a `single item ' on the basis of 10% as at (a) above, works out to less than Rupees one lakh, import would be permitted upto a value of Rs. 1 lakh provided it is within the overall flexibility allowed on the licence and (iii) import of non OGL capital goods (other than those appearing in Appendices 1 Part A and 8) without indigenous clearance, subject to the same conditions as stipulated at (ii) above within the entire flexibility allowed to Export/Trading Houses. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant, of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licence. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that petitioners had failed to diversify their export of "Other products" during the year 1977 78. The order refusing the Export Certificate was challenged by the petitioners by filing writ petitions under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Bombay High Court. One Writ Petition (filed by the Petitioners in writ petition No. 460 of 1988) was dismissed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court and the said orders were confirmed by the Division Bench of the Bombay, which held that the grantees of the Additional Licences were not only prohibited from importing items which were excluded under the Export Policy 1978 79 but also from importing articles excluded under Import Policy prevailing at the time of import and that the word "banned" was intended to take in terms which were banned altogether as well as items which are banned for import by the holder of an Additional Licence, and that there was no basis for classifying such Export Houses into two different categories on the date of issuance of the Addl Licences or on the strength of the period of exports against which such licences have been issued and that such a classification has no connection whatsoever with the object sought to be achieved by the Import & export Policy 1988 91. The High Court further directed the authorities to grant Export House Certificates to the petitioners under the Import Export Policy, 1978 79 within three months. While giving the said direction the High court imposed a condition in 237 the same terms as laid down by this Court in its order dated April 18, 1985, referred to above.

The petitioner was an Under Secretary to the Government of India in the Ministry of Shipping and Transport and on May 21, 1974 accepted employment as Joint Manager in the Mogul Line Limited, a Government of india undertaking after obtaining release from government service. He was first allotted a service quarter. In 1975 the company purchased a spacious flat being flat No. 151 in Jolly Maker apartment III at 119 Cuffe Parade and the petitioner being the senior most executive was allotted the flat for his residence. The petitioner retired from the service of the company on or about September 30, 1984. Prior to that i.e. On September 26, 1984 he addressed a letter requesting the company to permit him to continue to live in the company 's premises during the period of his accumulated leave after his retirement and in accordance with the company rules, he was required to pay compensation for the use of the premises. After the expiry of the said period of six months, the company addressed a letters requesting the petitioner to vacate the flat stating that if he failed to do so, he would be liable to pay higher compensation as per the company"s rules. Since the petitioner failed to vacate, the Company initiated proceedings for his eviction under the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised occupants) Act, 1971. The Estate Officer by order dated December 2, 1985 directed the eviction of the petitioner. The Petitioner filed a suit in the Court of Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate 37th Court Esplanade, Bombay alleging that he was wrongfully withholding the flat in question which had been given to him for his own residence during the periods of his employment and thereby committed an offence punishable under section 630 of the Act. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the view expressed by the Single Judge following the earlier decisions of the High Court in Amritlal Chum vs Devi Devi Ranjan Ranjan Ranjan Jha, ; , that it refers only to the existing officers and employees of a company within the ambit of section 630 was limited to such property of the Company which was wrongfully obtained by an officer or employee of the companies. The High Court dismissed the special leave petition filed by the petitioner under Article 226 of the Constitution and held that the construction placed by the High court on the provisions contained in section 630(1) of the is the only construction possible construction possible. In the Special Leave Petition it was contended for the petitioner that the provision contained in Section 630 of tho Act is a penal provision and therefore must be subject to a strict construction and there is no room for intendment. It was further submitted that on a true construction, the scope and effect of the section was limited only to such properties of the Companies which was illegally obtained by the officer or employees of the firm and not to those whose employment has been terminated. The beneficent provision contained therein in Section 630(1), namely, where an officer and employee of a Company wrongfully withholds possession of property of a public company, or (b) having obtained such property during the course of his employ, to which he is not entitled; and that both clauses (a) and (b), are separated by the word 'or ' and therefore are clearly disjunctive.

The appellant was the founder of a private temple. The deity installed in the temple according to religious rites. He also acquired certain properties and the said temple with the properties constituted Shri Vithal Rukhamai Sansthan of Amalner. After the passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, 1950, an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons Bhaskarrao Chimanrao Deshmukh, Ramrao Deshmukh and Ramkrishna Tryambak Deshpande as constituted attorneys of Vasudeobuwa who was described in the application as the "owner" of the property. The word 'Buwa ' means a place by whatever designation known and used as a place of public religious worship and dedicated to or for the benefit of or used as of right by the Hindu community or any section thereof as a Place of public Religious worship. The appellant contended that it was a private religious endowment and not a public one. He further submitted that there was no evidence of long user of this temple by the public as a matter of right. Held, that the deity installed by the Founder had become full owner thereof. In order to facilitate worship by the Public, the founder also intended that regular Bhajan, Kirtan and worship shall be maintained and annual ceremonies and processions for pilgrimage shall be conducted by the saints in succession nominated by the reigning saint. (3) There has been no evidence that the endowment was in favour of the deity or Sansthan or temple but in favour thereof by one Daryao Gir who was maintaining a temple and to his heirs in perpetuity, this Court further held in the above decision: "But, in the present case all the tests are fulfilled. To sum up from the documentary and oral evidence produced, the following features are present in the case: (1) The deity erected in the Temple was intended by the founder to be continually worshipped by an indeterminate multitude of the Hindu public; (2) In order that the founder should perform the Bhajan as was being done as per the Shishya Sampradaya and perform the cast in Chaturmas at Shrificer Pandharpur regularly and there after you should come to Amal and keep up the practice of celebrating the festivals etc. of Shri Sakharam Maharaj regularly as was going on; (3 ) The founder should pay the income of the said property for the purpose of Naivadya for the Deity Pandurang at night that day; (4) There had been no cross examination of any witness to show that it ever treated as a private property; and (5) The evidence of Ramkrishna Deshpande in his evidence, therefore, was without any force.

Section 46(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, which is impugned before this Court runs as follows: "46. . . . (2) The Income tax Officer may forward to the Collector a certificate under his signature specifying the amount of arrears due from an assessee, and the Collector on receipt of such certificate shall proceed to recover from such assessee the amount specified therein as if it were an arrear of land revenue. " The assessee was arrested on the 1st July 1955. On the 1 st February 1954, the Additional Collector issued a warrant for the arrest of the assessee under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring him to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said certified demand. The assessee did not appear in person but on the next day, the 17th June, 1955, an Advocate acting on behalf of the asses see, wrote a letter to the Additional District Collector purporting to show cause as why he was arrested and detained in jail in execution of a warrant of arrest issued under section 46(1) of Bombay City Act, 1882. The order was confirmed by the Additional Commissioner on the 30th March 1955. The sale proclamation was held on the 25th February 1955 fetching a price of Rs. 33,000 and it was confirmed on the 10th April, 1951. The sales were held on a single day fetching the price of RS. 33 lakhs and it Was confirmed on that date. The Sales Tax Officer issued a notice under section 12 of the Act requiring the assessee to appear in persons on the 15th January 1955 and called upon him to showcause why he be not apprehended and confine to civil prison in satisfaction with the said order. The respondent challenged the validity of the sale proclamation on the ground that it offended article 14 of the Constitution as the same was repugnant to article 14 Of the Constitution. Held, that the sale was not a sale within the meaning of section 46 (2). The sale was actually held after the date of amendment and the sale in question was validly held after that date and the Sales Tax Authorities were precluded from making any law with respect to income tax on the same date.

The appellants are the trustees of the Port of Bombay. The respondents to this appeal are the Trustees of the port of Bombay, who were represented by the Port Trust Employees ' Union. The dispute in the present case was whether the existing system of work needed any modification and that the so called period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end depending on the tides or the exigencies of the work. The Trustees first introduced a new system of working in the Alexandra Docks on June 30, 1953 and the same system was extended to the Prince 's and Victoria Docks and thereafter they were called out at any hour of the day or night. When the two shift system began, each shift of 12 hours was broken up into 8 hours ' duty, 2 hours ' rest at variable times and 2 hours ` overtime were prescribed. The workmen challenged the validity of the new system on the ground that it was a device to get 4 hours ' overtime and that as the lock gates control the depth of water in the Camandra Crew could not be maintained from day to day except in the monsoon months when the storm gates had some time to be closed. The Tribunal accepted the entire case put forward on behalf of the Trustees and the Union appealed to this Court. On behalf of them it was contended that (1) the change of 12 hour ' shift into 8 days ' duty by interposing intervals for rest, if owing to the nature of the works there is difficulty in giving the intervals for end in that manner on any particular day; (2) the period of work of adult workers in a factory each day shall be so arranged that inclusive of the intervals of rest shall not go beyond 12 hours. The contention of the workmen was that section 13 fixed the number of hours in a normal working day and this number is inclusive of one or more specified intervals, and (3) the introduction of variable recess does not satisfy the requirements of rest which is the basis for fixing statutorily the hours of work in relation to wages. HELD : (i) The provisions of the Minimum Wages Act, 1950 are not as clear as the corresponding provisions of section 13(2)(c) read with section 13 (3). [638 B] (ii) The scheme of the compels the inclusion of an hour of rest in a ' normal workingday because the total number of work hours in 6 a week cannot go beyond 48. What has not been done by the Act or the Rules is to specify that the interval for rest shall break up the hours Of work. [639 C] (iii) The workmen compared the case of the Prince "s andation Docks with the cases of the Alex andra Dock and the Flotilla Crew have to remain on duty for full 12 hours and they work as and when they are required. Although their hours of duty are only 8 they are entitled, if present for work, overtime up to four hours. [643 G] (iv) The workers are guilty of infraction of the by keeping the recess variable so long as they specify in advance the rectifess on any specific day. It will also be noticed that the scheme of compels the deletion of an " hour of ' rest in normal working days because the actual number of duty in a six day cannot go upto beyond 48 hours.

The respondent instituted a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely Abdul Rahim, Abdul Gaffur and Abdul Gafur from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1, Shibtola Lane), Calcutta. In the plaint itself, the first two defendants were described as thika tenants. No claim was made for rents or taxes although it was alleged that the same were in arrears. The suit was contested only by the third defendant who filed a written statement contending that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The trial court decreed the suit on March 18, 1949 after the Calcutta Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 had come into force and substituted a new definition of thika tenant. On appeal, the Subordinate Judge held that at the time when the appeal of the defendant was disposed of by the Subordinate judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Thika Tenant Act of 1948 and the definition of a thika tenancy in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. In second appeal, a single Judge of the High Court held that the question whether the appellant was entitled to the benefit of that Act had to be re examined and consequently he remanded the matter to the lower appellate court with a direction that there should be a fresh decision of the case after considering the law applicable and taking further evidence if necessary. On remand, the subordinate Judge held on the ground that at that time when appeal of defendant was heard for the second time, the right of the landlord to recover possession had not been given. The High Court also held that section 4 of the Act would be applicable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that with the omission of section 29 civil courts became unable to remit ejectment suits to the controller with the result that the Act as finally amended could not apply to pre suit suits and thika tenancies could get no relief under the Act. HELD: (i) The legislature had not intended to impose a bar or a qualification to the rights Of the parties by the use of suitable words such as "notwithstanding any law to the contrary or in any agreement between the parties". [176 B] (ii) Section 4 of that section should also be held to be prospective only. It could not be said that the legislature intended that a party who under a contract made prior to the Act had as perfect title to recover a sum of money as he had to any of his personal property, should be totally deprived of it without compensation. [176 C] (iii) The language of sections 4 and 5 leaves no room for doubt that after the coming into force of the , it was not open to the landlord either to allege any of the grounds specified in section 3 or to prove the existence thereof at the hearing of the suit, he had, to establish the existence of such a ground when the suit is heard. The ground need not be specified in the plaint but nevertheless it had to he established in the suit. [177 D] (iv) Section 5 lays down in clear terms that a "landlord wishing to eject a th kika tenant" on one or more of the three grounds specified therein "shall apply in the prescribed manner to the Controller". This is only consistent with the wish of a landlord after the Act has come into operation. [178 G] (v) The effect of omission of Section 28 has been considered by this Court in Mahadeolal Kanodia vs Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , followed.

Prior to 1965 in the High Court of Allahabad, Secretaries were on a higher pay scale than that of Section Officers. They were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs 120 300 300 to Section Officers Officers. In 1965 the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference ranging from Rs. 150 350 for Section Officers and Rs. 15 715 respectively. The Committee was asked to consider the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. It was required to consider and recommend changes to reduce the number of then existing pay scales. It recommended that ten posts of Bench Secretaries should be upgraded and placed in the Pay scale ofRs.500 1,000 as recommended by the Pay Commission. The State Government accepted the recommendations. Subsequently, these pay scales were raised to Rs. 200 450 and Rs 15 715. The High Court upheld their claim but half heartedly. The appellant filed a writ petition in the Allahabad High Court challenging the validity of bifurcation of one cadre into Grade I and Grade II. The petition was contested by the State contending that (1) the Bench Secretaries cannot be given the same scale of pay which is being given to Superintendents or the Section Officers; and (2) the creation of two Grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Secretary who are doing the same or similar work is violative of the right to have equal pay for equal work. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Pay Commission refused to equate Bench Secretaries with Section Officers in view of their differential duties. It is found that the nature of work of Section officers was quite different and more onerous than that Of Bench Secretaries. Section Officers have to bear more responsibilities in their Sections. They have to exercise control over their subordinate. They had to prepare lengthy original notes in complicated matters. The Commission, therefore, recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that was given to Assistants of the Secretariat. [294G H] 2. It would be detrimental to the interest of the service itself. In all lndia Customs and Central Excise Stenographers Recognised) and Others vs Union of India and Ors., [1985] Suppl. 1 SCR 101, this principle has no mechanical application in every case of similar work. It has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitution. Article l4 permits reasonable classification founded on different basis. It cannot be denied that the quality of work performed by persons of longer experience is superior than the work of newcomers. Even in the same cadre will not amount to discrimination. The classification based on experience is a reasonable classification. It had a rational nexus with the object thereof. To hold otherwise, it would be injurious to the interests of the Service itself. [292G H; 293A] 3. In service matters, merit or experience could be the proper basis for classification to promote efficiency in administration. He or she learns also by experience as much as by other means.

Section 68 empowers the State Government to declare any area as a special area by issuing a notification. Section 55 provides that for every Special Area there shall be a Special Area development Authority consisting of a Chairman and such other members as the Government may determine from time to time. The Chairman and the members of the Development Authority are appointed by the State Govern ment. Section 69(d) confers upon the Development authority powers for the purpose of municipal administration and for the purposes connected with the matters aforesaid. The corresponding provision in Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956 is section 132(1)(a). The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries in Venkatagiri. On January 10, 1942, an agreement was entered into between the Rajah of Venkatagiri and one Sri Balumuri Nageswara Rao whereby the Raja agreed to give annual leases in respect of certain slate quarry within his estate for five years in succession commencing from February 1942 if the lease were given continuously for 5 years, then the lessee would be entitled at the end of the fifth year to obtain a lease from the Rajah for a period of 20 years commencing from the termination of the sixth year. On December 10, 1947, the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Raja to him. The Board of Revenue passed an order on December 27, 1955 declaring that the lease to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945 and that as the lease was for a periods exceeding one year it was not enforceable against the Government according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. On appeal by the Board of revenue, the Board held that the lessee had been given notice before such termination and that the appellant 's lease was valid. The appellant then filed writ petition in the High Court praying for a writ of mandamus directing the State of Andhra Pradesh to forbear from terminating his leasehold right in the slate mines and from interfering with his possession and working of the slates and other ancillary reliefs. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the termination was bad as it did not give three months ' notice to the lessee or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act. Held, that on a true construction of the provisions of the Madras Estates Land (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948, which were passed under the Government of India Act, 1935, did offend section 299 of that Act and expressly save those Acts. The Abolition Act was one of the Acts included in the Ninth Schedule and was protected by article 31B. A. M.S. V.M. & Co. vs The State of Madras, ; , followed.
